call.text: The first call reached Sam before its speaker could make it. The speaker is still unknown.

holding.title: The temporary hold
holding.text: A precisely defined connection can be held temporarily. It cannot safely turn a person into a component.

deadline.title: The thirteenth interval
deadline.text: The accumulating messages will complete their circuit at first light on Sunday.

anubis.title: Anubis and the crossing
anubis.text: Anubis keeps a particular road and its passengers. His crossing is a choice, not universal authority over every part of the Duat.

records.title: A correction leaves evidence
records.text: The original false entry remains visible beside the record challenging it.

acknowledgement.title: Received without continuation
acknowledgement.text: Celia Bell’s message finished without claiming its receiver.

routes.title: Connections are directional
routes.text: A route, an address and a person are different subjects for a holding mark.

release.title: The release sequence
release.text: Two defined ends and an open refusal: loosen the agreement instead of cutting the body carrying it.

ren.title: Names and identity
ren.text: A name matters to a person’s identity. Miso’s chosen present name can make room beside a name used to bind him.

eva.title: Eva’s first call
eva.text: The first call had an end. Later imitations do not establish the same person.

original_call.title: The call she chose to finish
original_call.text: Eva left a message and chose to leave. Voss kept reopening its route.

wren.title: Wren
wren.text: She chose her own name. She carries intercepted voices but is not Eva Voss.

receiving_record.title: An independent receiving record
receiving_record.text: Wren can be recognised separately from the messages she carries.

reeds.title: A field with work to do
reeds.text: The Field of Reeds is encountered as a lived place, not a waiting room for somebody else’s grief.

wepwawet.title: Wepwawet: Opener of the Ways
wepwawet.text: Knowing which divine name and office to address can open an informed request. It does not confer ownership of a god.

true_mark.text: The false copy has a reversed final stroke. The original remains scratched underneath it.

recap.text: You tried to silence the first call.
You delivered a private letter without reading it.
You left a letter waiting while you pursued the rescue.
You chose Julian over a useful component.
You put the false record on the record.
You kept your mother’s recording instead of obtaining a witness seal.
You stayed for Imani’s selection session.
You cleared the playback that could be used to imitate Eva.
Knowledge opened a road that force could not.
Trying to force the road left an injury.
You refused divine terms and took the flooded bypass.
You returned the voices and brought your mother home.
You saved those present and cut off unfinished messages.
You stayed to receive the voices under terms you chose.
Imani remembered the clue you denied having.
You asked Wren for help before treating her as a tool.

beats.text: You had checked the hallway before turning the lock. Mrs. Rinaldi's shopping trolley stood beside the lift, and somebody had left a wet glove on top of the recycling box. Nobody else was there. You remember this with the unfair clarity that arrives when you need a different explanation.
Now the phone is ringing in your hand, showing tomorrow's date.

It is Friday. You check the little date above the microwave, which has said January 1 since a power cut two winters ago. Useless. The laptop on the kitchen table says Friday. The chemistry worksheet underneath it says your name, Sam Mansour, and beside the first question you've written a number you already know is wrong.
Outside, someone knocks three times.

Your aunt has a key. You tell yourself she could have lost it. Leila loses pens, hair ties, the small scissors she buys to replace the small scissors she loses. She has never lost her keys. They hang from a bright orange strap marked EMERGENCY, which she chose because, in her words, nobody steals something that looks like a responsibility.
The sound comes again. Patient. You put the phone down on the counter without ending the call.
“Leila?”
“Open up, Sam.”
Your own voice. Not a recording played back through a speaker. A person with your voice, out in the hallway, standing approximately where Mrs. Rinaldi parks her trolley.
You step away from the door. One of your socks catches a splinter in the laminate and makes a small, ordinary ripping sound.

There are things you can do. Your aunt has spent eleven months providing lists of them. If you're frightened, call me. If you can't sleep, put on that boring history podcast. If you hear something outside, use the peephole, don't start an argument through the door. A plan for every emergency she can name.
Through the peephole, a person in your winter coat is holding a phone to their ear.

You know it is your coat because of the triangular patch near the pocket, where Mum fixed a tear with a scrap from an old curtain. A grey curtain with yellow birds. You had complained that it looked like something for a five-year-old, then refused to let her replace it.
The person raises their eyes to the peephole.
For a moment your brain does something embarrassing. It tries to make this a mirror. It adjusts the height, the angle, the shape of the light. Then the person smiles while your mouth stays open.
You cover the peephole with your palm.
On the kitchen counter, your phone says, “Sam?”
You don't remember deciding to pick it up.
“I'm here.”
The breath at the other end catches. Behind it, water runs over something hollow. A bell rings once, far away.
“Whatever happens,” your voice says, “do not open the door.”
You look at the door. The lock is turning slowly. You can see the little brass tab moving, fraction by fraction, although there is no key on your side.
“How do I stop it?”
“Blue notebook. Kitchen drawer.”
“What?”
“Mum's notebook. Get it. And Sam—”
The line goes dead.

For eleven months, adults have paused before saying your mother's name. Your teachers do it. Your dentist once did it with two fingers in your mouth, which made you briefly, furiously glad she hadn't gone into medicine. They say missing, and then wait to find out what version of that word you're living with today.
The voice on the phone said Mum as if she could still come into the kitchen and tell you to stop picking the bird patch off your coat.
You open the drawer under the kettle.

Takeaway menus. A packet of birthday candles. Elastic bands Leila insists are useful, although their main function is to attach themselves to everything else. Under a bent photograph of you at a science fair lies a blue cloth notebook.
You've searched this drawer before. Twice. Once for a tin opener, once because you thought Mum might have left something your aunt hadn't found.
The notebook is warm.
You turn back its cover. Nadia Mansour, it says. If found, please return. Then her email address, the one you still sometimes write messages to and leave in drafts.
Beneath that, in a different pen: Sam, if you're reading this, find Leila before you try anything clever.

Your knees go unreliable. You sit down on the edge of a chair and read the line twice. It is recognisably her handwriting, including the dot she always puts too far to the right of an i. You press your thumb against it, hard enough to crease the page.
The lock clicks.

You push the chair under the door handle. It fits badly. Leila has told the landlord six times that the kitchen chairs are too wobbly to use safely. Tonight you would like them to be considerably less affordable.
“Sam,” the person outside says. “You left me out here.”
“You're wearing my coat.”
“So are you.”
You look down. The coat is over the chair at the table, exactly where you left it after school.
A little black paw appears outside the kitchen window and taps the glass.

You turn so quickly the notebook falls shut. On the fire escape sits a cat, fur puffed out against the cold. It has one pale whisker, a nick in an ear and the offended expression of an animal who has been waiting a long time.
It taps again.
You can hear the chair scraping across the floor behind you.
The window has been painted shut at the bottom. You hook your fingers under the frame and pull. Nothing. The cat mouths something through the glass. You stare at it.
It rolls its eyes, leans closer and says, distinctly, “Latch.”
You undo the latch.
The frame shoots upward. Cold air stings the wet inside of your nose. The cat climbs over the sill, shakes snow onto the chemistry worksheet, and pushes past you towards the notebook.
“Coat,” it says. “Phone. Shoes. Leave the laptop.”
You haven't mentioned the laptop.
“The expensive square,” the cat adds, impatiently. “Humans always go back for the expensive square.”
A screw falls from the door handle and bounces under the fridge.
You put on your coat. The real one, with the patch that catches on your thumb. You shove your feet into your boots, grab the notebook and phone, and climb through the window.
At the top of the fire escape, you look back.

Your door opens three inches against the chair. In the gap you see your own hand, then an eye. The person inside your apartment looks towards the window. Its mouth moves. You can't hear the words over the traffic below.
The cat bites your sleeve and pulls.
You follow it down.

choices.label: Follow the cat down the fire escape

beats.text: The first landing is iced over. You discover this by sitting down on it extremely quickly.

Pain shoots up your left elbow. You manage to keep hold of the notebook. Your phone slides three steps farther than you do and stops against a screw, which is the first useful screw you've encountered tonight.
The cat looks up from the next landing.
“Careful.”
You consider several responses. Your aunt would not approve of any of them, though she uses the most efficient one when the hospital calls during dinner.
You get up slowly. The apartment window above you goes dark.

At street level the ladder ends eight feet above a collection of bins. You have lived in this building for four years without once thinking about the last eight feet of the fire escape. Clearly somebody on a planning committee thought fire would get bored before then.
“There's a release,” a voice says below you.
A girl in a red parka stands beside the bins, one glove raised. In her other hand she holds a hockey stick with a strip of blue tape around the blade.
“By your right foot. No, your other right.”

You find the catch. The ladder drops with a crash that sets off a car alarm halfway down the alley. The cat disappears under a skip. You climb down into a puddle deep enough to find the gap between your jeans and boots.
The girl watches you inspect the wet hem.
“You're Sam?”
You have just been warned not to open a door by someone wearing your face. This seems like a poor time to start confirming personal information.
“Who's asking?”
“Imani. Third floor. Your aunt sent me.” She takes out her phone. There is a message from Leila: Can you check on Sam? Not answering. Don't go inside if anything seems off. Call me.
Underneath it, Imani has written: Off how.
Leila hasn't answered.

You check your own phone. Four missed calls from your aunt. One incoming call labelled tomorrow, with no number attached. You try to show Imani, but the date changes back to today as soon as she leans closer.
“That's convenient,” you say.
“What is?”
“Nothing.”
She slips the phone into her pocket. “Right. Well, I'm on my way to my dad's shop. He can drive us to your aunt.”
“At two in the morning?”
“He's finishing a bus. I was awake. Why are you coming out of a window?”
The cat emerges from under the skip with a yoghurt lid attached to its back foot. It pauses to shake it off, fails, and turns its entire body to bite it.
“That,” you tell Imani, “is a longer answer.”
She follows your gaze. The cat freezes with the lid in its mouth.
“Is it yours?”
“No.”
“Then why does it look like you owe it money?”

You take a breath. A man with a takeaway bag passes the mouth of the alley, glances at the two of you and the ladder, and continues without slowing. The car alarm stops. Above you, one of the apartment windows opens. Somebody shouts that people have work in the morning.
You want to be that person. You would like your part in tonight's events to involve being briefly annoyed, closing a window and going back to sleep.
Imani shifts her stick to the other hand. “Your elbow's bleeding.”
You look down. A thin dark line has reached the edge of your cuff.
“It's fine.”
“I'm sure. Are you coming?”

You recognise her now. She and her dad moved into the third floor in the autumn. Leila took them food, then complained for a week that she'd given away her best container. You met Imani by the lifts and asked whether she went to your school. She said yes. You said cool. Neither of you could think of a second subject, so you watched the lift numbers together until she got out.
She knows your name because Leila uses it through the wall. You know hers because you once collected a delivery meant for her dad and kept forgetting to take it downstairs.
It occurs to you that, before tonight, this was approximately the amount of friendship you could manage without somebody asking how you were.
Your phone rings.
Leila's face fills the screen, a photograph you took without warning while she was halfway through eating a peach. You answer so fast you almost drop it.
“I'm outside.”
“Outside where?”
“The building. There was someone—”
“Don't tell me your whole name. Don't tell anybody your whole name. Are you wearing the coat with the patch?”
You look at the bird.
“Yes.”
“Good. Keep it on. Imani there?”
Imani reaches for the phone. You put it on speaker instead.
“I'm here,” she says. “What's happening?”
Leila breathes out. In the background somebody calls for a porter.
“I need you both at the museum annex. The service door on the east side. Not the public museum. The little brick building across the lane. I'll send a pin.”
“Your shift?” you ask.
“I've asked somebody to cover.”
“Leila. There's someone in our flat.”
“I know.”
You stand very still. A drop of water falls from the end of the ladder onto your neck.
“How do you know?”
“We'll talk when you get here.”
“No. How—”
The call breaks into a rough crackle. You hear another voice through it, a girl's voice, very young. “Dad says don't tell them.”
Then the screen goes black.
Imani looks at you. The cat has stopped wrestling the yoghurt lid.
Behind the alley bins, the shadow cast by the streetlight lengthens until it reaches your boot. You move your foot. The shadow follows.
The cat drops the lid.
“Walk,” it says. “Don't run until you have to.”
For two seconds nobody moves.
Imani looks from you to the cat, then back again. She opens her mouth, closes it, and takes a firm grip on the hockey stick.
“Fine,” she says. “Museum. Talking later.”

choices.label: Ask Imani to come; share what you know

effects.detail: You asked for help instead of giving orders.

choices.label: Tell her to keep up; explain later

effects.detail: You ordered her to keep up in the alley.

beats.text: The pin Leila sends takes you to a brick building behind a locked vehicle gate. There is no sign saying museum annex, no golden mask on the door, nothing to explain why your aunt knows how to get in. A green wheelie bin lies on its side beside a pile of damp cardboard.
Imani presses the intercom.
A man answers, “Deliveries after eight.”
“Leila sent us.”
Nothing happens. You can hear a radio playing on the other side, followed by the scrape of a chair. Then the gate releases with a buzz.
“Nice security,” you say.
“The gate,” the man tells you through the intercom, “is on camera.”
You stop talking to the gate.

Inside the service entrance, the air smells of radiator dust and cardboard. A security officer sits behind a desk with a half-completed crossword. He has written the same answer in two different places and is frowning at one of them.
“She's downstairs. Don't touch anything. Cat stays out.”
The cat walks between his shoes.
He looks down at it. “You again.”
“Evening, Dennis.”
Dennis removes his glasses, rubs the bridge of his nose and puts them back on. “I've told them about this. They still won't put it in the incident form.”
You and Imani follow the cat before Dennis can remember you were supposed to be doing something ordinary.

The basement stairs end at a fire door propped open with a crate of bottled water. Leila stands beyond it in her navy scrubs, coat unbuttoned, her hair escaping its clip. She has one of the hospital's small cardboard cups in her hand. When she sees you she puts it down without finding a surface. It falls and spills coffee across the floor.

She hugs you first. You don't decide whether to let her. Her arms close around your shoulders and your face presses into the clean hospital smell of her sleeve, and for a second you stop holding yourself upright.
Then she takes your elbow.
“Sit.”
“I'm fine.”
“Sit while being fine.”

She cleans the cut with something from her bag. It hurts more than you expect. Imani leans her stick against the table and watches the door. The cat starts washing its chest as if it has done all the work available.
“You knew,” you say.
Leila peels the backing off a dressing.
“About that thing in the flat. You said you knew.”
“I knew it might try.”
The cat stops washing. Imani looks at you, then discreetly studies a shelf of archive boxes.
“How long?”
Leila presses the dressing down too firmly. You flinch, and she loosens her grip.
“Since your mum went missing.”

There is a notice on the wall asking staff to separate paper and plastic waste. You read it three times while she tells you that your mother studied things she couldn't put in published papers. That the little brick building stores equipment which isn't part of the museum's public collection. That some of the work happened here, after hours, with permission from people who knew enough to sign the right forms and not enough to be useful now.
“You let the police look for her.”
“Yes.”
“You let me go with them.”
“Sam.”
“I showed them her favourite coffee place.”
Leila puts the unused half of the dressing packet into her pocket. “I remember.”
You pull your arm away. “Were you ever going to tell me?”
She looks towards Imani. You hate her for that small glance, for measuring how much can be said in front of somebody else.
Imani picks up her stick. “There's a vending machine upstairs. I'm going to call my dad.”
Nobody asks her to leave. She goes anyway, letting the fire door close behind her with a gentle click.
Leila waits until it has shut. “I didn't know whether Nadia was alive.”
“But you knew where she'd gone.”
“I knew the name of a place. I couldn't reach it.”
“You could have told me that.”
“Yes,” she says.

The answer is so plain that for a moment you have nothing to put against it. You had prepared for excuses. You've spent eleven months listening to people explain how little information they can give you.
You put the notebook on the table. Her face changes when she sees it.
“Where did you find that?”
“In the drawer. Where you keep the menus.”
“It wasn't there.”
“I know.”

She sits down opposite you. Her hand hovers above the cover without touching it. You see a faint white scar across the inside of her wrist, one you asked about last summer. She said she'd burned herself with steam.
The cat jumps onto the table.
“He needs the diagram,” it says.
Leila's expression hardens. “You need to tell me how you got out.”
“I walked.”
“You don't walk.”
“I've been practising.”
Something taps against a cupboard door on the far wall. The cat lowers itself until its belly touches the table. Leila gets up at once.
“Stay there.”
Of course you don't.

Inside the cupboard is an old brass bell, the kind with a little button on top. It sits on a saucer of salt. Beside it lie a battery recorder, a length of cut telephone cable and a photograph of a girl in a yellow raincoat. Somebody has folded the photograph so tightly that a white line runs across the girl's face.
The bell's button pushes down.
Leila catches it before it can release.
A voice comes from the recorder, although its screen is off. You recognise the small voice from the interrupted call.
“Dad says we're not ready.”
The cat backs into your leg.
Leila holds the bell so tightly her hand shakes. “Sam. Open the notebook. First blue tab.”

You do. Under the tab is a drawing of a circle crossed by three short lines. One of the lines is broken. Beneath it, Mum has written: Temporary hold. Seven minutes maximum. Never use on living tissue.
You show Leila.
“I know what it looks like. Draw it.”
“With what?”
She nods at a box on the shelf. Inside are sticks of white chalk wrapped in tissue. Your fingers close around one and come away dusty.
You copy the circle on the cupboard's inside wall. The chalk squeaks. Nothing happens. Leila makes a small sound through her teeth.
“Close the end. It's open at the bottom.”
You repair the gap.
The bell stops moving. Leila takes her hand away. A red mark has appeared across her palm.
On the table, your phone lights up.
A message from an unknown number reads: Your mother is tired. We should discuss this before somebody makes a mistake.
The name beneath it is Adrian Voss.

You know the name Voss. It is on a plaque beside a lift in the museum, and on a Christmas card Mum used to stand behind the kettle because she didn't like the picture on the front. A silver deer, you remember. A deer with legs too long for the envelope.
Leila reads the message and turns your phone face down.
“Don't answer.”
“That's what everyone keeps saying about phones tonight.”

She takes a breath, stops, and goes to fetch another chair. There are several things she wants you to do with the chair, judging from the care with which she positions it. Sit. Stay still. Be younger.

Instead you open Mum's notebook. Behind the diagram you used is a map with three names you recognise and one you don't. The annex. A disconnected exchange room. A service building near the waterfront. The fourth name is written in a careful hand: Duat.
The cat puts a paw on the page.
“Other side,” it says. “Complicated place. Don't assume every door goes to the same part.”
“You're going to explain why you talk at some point.”
“I'm Miso. I talk because I have things to say.”
“You could say them better.”
Miso looks at Leila. “He's definitely hers.”
You aren't ready for anyone to make that observation, even a cat. You push his paw off the notebook.
Imani returns with a paper cup of hot chocolate and a packet of plain crisps. She sets the crisps beside you.
“My dad's coming here at five. He's finishing the bus first. He thinks your aunt's car broke down.” She looks at Leila. “I'd like to keep the rest of the lie small.”
Leila nods once. “You should go home with him.”
“Probably.” Imani sits on the table instead of the chair. “What was the ringing?”
Nobody answers quickly enough.
“Okay,” she says. “Still doing that.”

You turn the notebook so she can see the map. Leila's lips press together, but she lets you. You tell Imani about the double and the voice on the phone, including the part where it sounded like you. Saying it aloud in a lit room makes it sound less believable. Imani asks whether you checked the call log, then remembers she already watched you try.
Miso walks over the map.
“Nadia left a return address. We need to know whether it still receives.”
“Where?” you ask.
“The old exchange room. We take the streetcar.”
Leila begins to object. Miso looks towards the bell cupboard, where the chalk mark is already turning grey at its edges.
“If you leave that unattended,” he says, “we'll be finding out how many people in this city answer unknown numbers.”

She looks at you. You can see how badly she wants a reason to say no that you will accept. At last she takes your phone and enters a number, then presses a brass feather into your palm. It is small enough to fit between two fingers, with a hole drilled through the stem.
“Your mother's. Keep it. Call me from the exchange room, not on the way. If the screen starts showing dates it shouldn't, put it away.”
“Is Mum alive?”
“I don't know,” she says. “I am going to tell you what I know, even when it's that.”
You put the feather in the chalk box. It doesn't feel like enough to trust her with.
Outside, the cold has sharpened. Imani buys two fares from a machine while you try to work out what a cat pays. Miso climbs into the fold of your coat, apparently resolving the question.
The streetcar arrives almost empty. You check the destination display before boarding. It shows the right street, then a string of characters you can't read, then the right street again.
“We sure?” you whisper.
“Quite sure we shouldn't stand here,” Miso says from inside your collar.
Imani goes first. The driver holds up one hand.
“What did you leave behind?”
She looks at the fare reader. “We're paying.”
“Different question.”
The driver's face is hidden under the brim of his cap. His hands rest on a wheel that streetcars do not normally have. Behind him, rainwater moves upward across the windscreen.
Imani steps back until her elbow touches yours.
“The fare is an honest account,” the driver says. “Something unfinished. Something you can still name without taking it from anybody else.”
“Can we get off?” you ask.
“Yes.” He nods towards the open doors. “While they're open.”
That helps. You hadn't realised how badly you needed to hear a choice was actually yours.

You asked what the crossing would claim.

beats.text: The streetcar crosses a bridge you cannot see. Its wheels make the regular clatter of tracks, but beneath the windows there is only water and the occasional pale shape moving against the current.
Imani is still holding her fare.
“Do I need one of those transfers?” she asks.
“You'll need to tell me where you're going,” Anubis says.
“The exchange room.”
“Not an address I would recommend.”
Miso climbs from your coat onto the empty seat opposite. “The child has a return line.”
“Then the child should learn to use the return line.”
“Everyone's a teacher when they're driving.”
Anubis looks at him in the mirror. Miso lowers his ears and stops talking.

The boy holding the bread gets up at the next stop. Through the open door you see a narrow platform, a lamp and a woman standing with both hands over her mouth. The boy runs to her without looking back. By the time the doors shut, the platform has gone.
You lean forward.
“Can you take us to my mum?”
“No.”
The answer comes without hesitation. You wish he'd taken a little longer to find it.
“Don't you know where she is?”

“I know what your guide told me. I also know there are roads which turn anyone who travels them into part of the toll. I'm responsible for the passengers who use this road. That doesn't give me authority over every broken thing connected to it.”
He indicates the seats behind you. The woman with the suitcase looks away before you can meet her eyes.
You sit back. You hadn't realised you were asking him to leave other people waiting.
Miso paws at the transfer in your hand. The stamp looks like a feather enclosed by a rectangle. Under it, in ordinary English, someone has written RECEIVED WITHOUT SUBSTITUTE.
“Keep that,” he says.
“What substitute?”
“Ask the man who sent you a message.”

You look at the place where a stamped transfer might have been. Miso follows your gaze. “We can still find the door,” he says. “Don't assume the route will remember us as invited.” You put the blank fare ticket in your pocket and leave the thought there with it.
Imani has been watching the river. “Does everybody end up here?”
Anubis takes a long moment before answering her.
“People have imagined many roads. People have needed many roads. This is one of mine.”
At the next stop he opens the doors and points to a concrete staircase.
“Up. Keep to the rail. Don't answer anyone who asks you to hold their place.”

You want to ask what happens if you do. Miso is already out of the streetcar, his claws clicking on the concrete. Imani follows. You thank the driver, feel foolish thanking a god as if he's held a door for you, then feel more foolish for thinking the two things should cancel each other out.
“Sam,” he says.
You turn.
“An address brings you to a door. It doesn't decide whether you open it.”
Before you can ask if that is advice about the call, the doors close.
At the top of the stairs you find a locked metal door. Beside it is a disconnected payphone. The receiver hangs crookedly from a cord wrapped in silver tape.
Miso jumps onto the little shelf under it. “Notebook.”
You find the return address. It isn't a building number. It is a sequence of six marks, three of which you recognise from the temporary hold.
“Say them?” you ask.
“Dial them.”

The keypad has no numbers. When you look closely you can see scratches where numbers should be, shapes that rearrange when you stop concentrating. You turn the notebook to match their orientation and press the sequence.
The call connects on the fifth mark.
“No,” Miso says quickly. “Finish it.”
A woman's voice says, “Sam?”
Your finger stops above the last key.
“It's Mum. Listen. I don't have long.”

You know the voice. It has the little rough place at the bottom that arrived after she had a winter cough three years ago. You know how she says listen before telling you where she put something you should already have found.
Imani touches your wrist.
“Six marks,” she says. “There are six.”
The receiver has gone warm.
“Mum?”
Miso's claws press into the back of your hand. He isn't hurting you. He is close to it.
“Last mark.”
You press it.
The voice cuts off halfway through your name. A mechanism turns inside the door, and a young man on the other side pulls it open.
He is wearing a cardigan with one elbow held together by safety pins. His hair is flattened on one side as if he has been asleep against a book.
“You nearly sent your return line through an open channel,” he says. Then he notices Miso. “Oh, good. It's your fault.”
“Julian,” Miso says.
“Don't Julian me. I've been here since Wednesday.”
He lets you in. Beyond the door lies a room full of empty telephone booths. Their glass panels reflect a sky full of stars, although there are no windows.
One booth at the back is lit. In it, a telephone rings beneath a handwritten sign.
DO NOT PICK UP TO SEE WHO IT IS.
Underneath, someone has added: YES, THIS MEANS YOU, JULIAN.
Julian puts the kettle on, checks the water level, and takes it off again.
“Never mind. It might be river water.”

You follow his gaze to a stain on the ceiling. It has the shape of the building above you, though the building changes while you watch. A chimney disappears. A fire escape grows down through one edge. Your own kitchen window opens briefly in the middle.
“Is that how you saw the flat?” you ask Miso.
He jumps onto a desk and settles his tail over his paws. “One way.”
Julian makes a sound that suggests there are several worse ways.

He is nineteen, he tells you, studying part-time and working for the small independent archive attached to the annex. He says independent with a care that suggests he has already had to explain it to a tax office. Most of the collection is ordinary: old operator manuals, repair logs, donated equipment. The part that isn't ordinary has been making his working week increasingly difficult.
“My supervisor used to deal with that bit.”
“Nadia?”
He nods.
“You knew my mum.”
“I still know her.”
For that sentence alone, you could forgive him a lot. He seems to realise he has offered something larger than he meant to, because he begins moving papers into neat piles.
The lit booth rings again.
Imani points to it. “What happens if somebody picks up?”
“Usually someone asks for somebody who isn't there. If you tell them they're wrong, they try the next place. If you offer to help, the system decides you're available.”
“Available for what?”
Julian looks at Miso.
The cat answers. “To carry the message.”
He says it as if that should explain everything. You wait until he notices you haven't understood.
“The original line let a caller send a message without making the receiver answer. Whoever built this version removed that safeguard.”
Julian takes a recorder from a drawer. It is the same model as the one in the annex. A strip of tape on its back says NADIA: BACKUP.
Your mother speaks when he presses play.

“Test forty-three. The holding mark remains temporary. Seven minutes if the line is stable. Less if it isn't. We need a second reader at the receiving end. Adrian says we can automate the acknowledgement. I disagree.”
A pause. A paper being turned. In the background you hear yourself, younger, complaining about homework. Julian stops the recorder when he sees your face.
“Sorry.”
“Play it.”
“There's quite a lot.”
“Play it.”

Mum's voice returns. She describes a circuit she has been testing, then corrects herself, then starts the explanation again without recording over the first attempt. You have spent months trying to preserve every memory you have of her. Here she is getting annoyed at a loose battery cover.
You need to sit down. You do it before anybody asks.
The recording ends with her saying, “Sam, don't put that near the—” and a loud clatter.

You remember the day. You dropped a screwdriver into a ceramic mug she'd been using to hold broken components. You thought she was angry because it was her favourite mug. Now, listening to the quick movement afterwards, you wonder what else was inside it.
Julian slides the recorder across the desk.
“Keep it. It's a copy.”
“Why haven't you given this to Leila?”
His mouth tightens.
“Because I couldn't get back through the door until someone dialled the full return address. I did tell you about Wednesday.”
Miso examines a paw.
You take the chalk from its box. On the desk you draw the holding mark, exactly as you drew it in the cupboard. Julian sets an old desk fan beside it and plugs the fan into a socket. Nothing happens.
“Magic doesn't work because chalk is expensive,” he says. “That shape holds a relationship. You need to tell it what relationship.”
You point to the notebook. “It doesn't say that.”
“It does. In the little note you skipped.”
It does. You skipped the note because it looked like a caption.

He puts your hand on the fan's plug, then makes you describe the connection between the socket and the motor. You say electricity. He asks what electricity is doing. You say making the fan spin. He asks what you want to stop.
“The fan spinning.”
“Then you want the mechanism, not the connection.”
Imani, who has been crouching beside the fan, turns its power switch on. It begins to rattle.
“Or that,” Julian says.

You let go of the plug. You want to laugh, but the room has started to feel unfair. Your mother did something here that kept her away for eleven months. There should be a more difficult explanation than a switch you didn't notice.
Julian tears a sheet of paper in half and writes YOUR END on one piece, MY END on the other. He gives one to you.
“Try it on something that needs two people.”
You put the paper on the desk. Imani holds the second half. When you close the final line of the chalk mark, the two pieces rise an inch from the wood and stay there.
Your fingers ache. You concentrate on the torn edges, on where they would fit together. The paper begins to shake.
“Breathe,” Imani says.
You breathe. The pieces settle.
Julian starts a timer. You hold the mark for forty-one seconds before your hand cramps and the papers fall.
It feels like failure until he writes forty-one in the margin beside your mother's first test.
Her time was twelve seconds.
At the back of the room, the ringing phone stops. A printer you hadn't noticed begins feeding out paper. Julian reaches it before the sheet can fall.
Three lines are printed across the top.
RECEIVING POINT CONFIRMED.
NADIA MANSOUR: CONNECTION ACTIVE.
COLLECTION SCHEDULE: SUNDAY, FIRST LIGHT.
It is Friday morning. You have two days.
The collection schedule gives you a deadline and no address. You turn the paper over as if the missing information might be on the back.
Julian takes it away before you wear a hole through it.
“We have to trace an earlier call. Same receiving point, older sender. There'll be an acknowledgement.”
“An address.”
“If the operator kept records.”
“Did she?”
He raises one eyebrow at the notebook in your hand.

Miso leads you to a booth with a cracked pane. Behind the glass, a telephone sits beside a sewing basket. An empty chair faces a window full of afternoon sunshine. It is bright enough to make your eyes hurt after the long night.
“This was Celia Bell's,” Julian says. “A volunteer operator. She died before the connection broke. Her channel's been replaying because the last message never reached its destination.”
“Where's Celia?”
“Gone on. This is what she left.”
He doesn't offer a simpler explanation. You are beginning to appreciate that about him.

The door opens into a flat full of warm air and the smell of something baking. A radio plays softly in the kitchen. There are birthday cards on the mantelpiece, several months of them displayed together. On the table beside the telephone lies an envelope addressed to a man called Martin.
A woman in a green cardigan sits by the window. When you come in, she looks up and smiles.
“Are you from the pharmacy?”
“No,” you say.
“I rang yesterday. They said they'd send somebody.”
Imani stays in the doorway. Miso sniffs the woman's shoes, then moves to the telephone.
The woman doesn't react to him. She repeats her question.
“Are you from the pharmacy?”
You understand then, a little. The room is starting over. The radio plays the same two notes. The kitchen clock clicks back from twelve to eleven.
On the envelope, the ink of Martin's name runs down the paper.
Julian points towards a cabinet behind the woman's chair. “Routing book. We need the entries for last March.”

You could walk around her. She isn't watching you; her gaze is fixed on the door, waiting for a person who must be taking a long time. But her hand rests on the cabinet's drawer, and when Julian tries to open it she grips the handle.
“Private papers.”
“We need to help someone.”
“Private papers,” she says again.
You look at the letter. The envelope hasn't been sealed. A faint rectangle marks the place where a stamp should be.
“Who is Martin?” you ask.
The radio stops.
“My son.”
“Can we deliver your letter?”
For the first time her eyes follow you. They are a cloudy blue, with the red rims of someone who hasn't slept well.
“He doesn't answer the phone.”
“Do you have his address?”
She gestures to the envelope. The street name has almost disappeared. You write it down before it can go entirely.
Julian shifts his weight. “Sam. We can't start taking on every—”
“I said can we. I haven't said I will.”
Mrs. Bell looks towards the kitchen. A timer sounds once and dies.
“I told him not to come,” she says. “He was driving in that weather. I said it could wait until Tuesday.”
You sit on the edge of the sofa. The cushion has a dent where someone must have sat for years.
“Did he come?”
“No.”
She looks relieved, and then unhappy, and then relieved again. The room doesn't seem able to decide which part to keep.
Imani takes out her phone. There is no signal, but she types the address into a note.
“We can find out whether he still lives there,” she says. “That's a thing we can actually promise.”
Mrs. Bell releases the drawer.

Inside, the routing book is an ordinary ledger with ruled columns. Most of the entries are numbers. In the margin beside Nadia Mansour, a small cross has been drawn through the return line. Under it, your mother's writing says: Received at lower station. Witness present: A. Voss. Ask why he didn't sign.
You photograph the page. On your screen, the photograph shows only a blank ledger.
“Pen,” Julian says, passing you one. “Paper holds. Cameras copy the wrong layer.”
You write the entry in your notebook, including the little cross and the exact position of the unsigned box.
The woman reaches for the letter. Her fingers go through it.
“Oh,” she says.
The afternoon light thins.
Miso stands beside the door, tail rigid. “We should leave.”

The room has begun to tilt. Cups slide across the mantelpiece. Imani catches your sleeve as the sofa shifts away from the wall. You take the envelope with your other hand and pull back towards the booth.
Mrs. Bell has stopped looking at you. She is watching the window.
“Tell him it wasn't because I didn't want him,” she says.
You cannot tell whether she's asking you or remembering a conversation she already had.
Back in the exchange room, the glass pane cracks from top to bottom. The flat goes dark. Your watch says six minutes and forty-eight seconds have passed.
You still have the letter.
Julian closes the booth door carefully.
“You're going to need to decide,” he says, “which promises fit in two days.”
You put the envelope inside the notebook, where the address won't rub away.

effects.detail: You delivered Celia Bell’s letter without reading it.

effects.detail: Celia Bell’s letter is still waiting to be delivered.

beats.text: The letter has an address on a street Julian says isn't far from the exchange room's ordinary exit. It is still early enough that the shops have their shutters down. You stand under an awning while a delivery driver drags crates into a bakery and wonder whether showing up at a stranger's house before seven counts as a worse idea when the letter comes from his dead mother.
Imani checks the note in her phone.
“We can leave it. We promised to find out whether he lives there. Not make him open it.”
Julian is carrying the evidence box against his chest. He has been looking at the time every few minutes.
“Your aunt thinks we're on our way back.”
“So tell her where we are,” Imani says.
You do. Leila replies with an address confirmation and a request to stay together. No lecture. It is almost more difficult to argue with.

The house has a small front garden full of snow-covered pots. Two bins stand by the side gate. A light is on in the kitchen. Through the glass beside the door you can see a coat rack with far more coats than the space was designed to hold.
You ring once.
A man in slippers opens the door. He looks at the three of you, then at the box, then at Miso. His hand stays on the latch.
“Yes?”
“Martin Bell?”
“Who's asking?”

Fair question. You give your first name and explain that the letter was found among papers belonging to his mother. It is a careful explanation. You don't enjoy how much it resembles Leila's earlier ones.
He looks at the envelope.
“My mother died in November.”
“We know.”
He takes it, examines the handwriting and leans one shoulder against the door frame. For a moment he seems too tired to keep being suspicious.
“Where was this?”
“In an archive,” Julian says. “She worked as a volunteer operator. We're cataloguing a group of personal papers.”
Not entirely true. Not entirely false. Martin looks at the box again and accepts enough of it to stop asking at the door.
He doesn't invite you in. You are glad. It means you don't have to explain which part of your reason for being there is a trespass into his life.
He turns the envelope over. The back is unsealed.
“Did you read it?”
“No,” you say.

You could have. In the exchange room, during the long wait for the door. In Dennis's car. On the pavement. The notebook has been full of things you needed to know, and it would have been easy to put the letter in the same category.
Martin nods once. He opens it while you stand on the step. His eyes move quickly over the first lines, then stop.
Behind him, someone in the kitchen asks whether he needs help. He says no without looking away from the page.
You feel you should leave. Nobody has told you to leave. You have become very aware of the wet soles of your boots and the small stone under one heel.
Then Martin folds the letter.
“She kept telling me not to drive in the snow,” he says.
You don't answer. You know something he hasn't asked you to know, and saying it would make you the owner of a conversation that belongs to him.
He looks at the envelope again.
“I was angry. I thought she didn't want help. She always made it sound like a nuisance, having somebody come over.”
Imani shifts beside you. Julian studies a crack in the step.
Martin rubs his thumb along the fold.
“Thank you for bringing it.”
“You're welcome.”
He goes inside. The door closes gently. You hear a chair move in the kitchen, then another voice, too low to understand.
On the pavement, you take out your notebook to mark the promise complete. Your pen hovers above the page.
Julian says, “Don't write what he said.”
“I wasn't.”
You had been about to. Not from malice. It was a clue, a response, something that might help explain the system. You close the notebook and put it away.
Miso walks beside the garden wall. His paws make four precise prints in the new snow. You watch them until the next patch of cleared pavement makes them disappear.

At the corner, Imani buys three small buns from the bakery. Julian says he doesn't want one, then eats half before remembering he said that. You stand under the awning, eating warm bread while the delivery driver restacks his empty crates.
“Was it worth the time?” Julian asks.
You think of Mum in a room you haven't reached yet. The deadline. The narrow places a day can acquire when you're afraid of using it badly.
“I don't know how to count it.”
He accepts that. You are grateful he doesn't tell you the answer should be obvious.
On your phone, the routing entry for Celia Bell changes. A small line of text appears beneath it: received without continuation.
You show Julian. He stops eating.
“That,” he says, “is what the acknowledgement is supposed to look like.”
You write down those words. Not Martin's letter. Not his grief. Just the part the line has given you permission to see.
When you reach the annex, Leila is standing outside the door. She looks at the time, at the three of you, and then at the bag from the bakery.
“Any left?”
Imani hands her the last bun. Your aunt eats half of it before asking for the report.

Leila collects you from the service door of a building you could have walked past a hundred times. She has borrowed Dennis's car, an elderly hatchback with a child seat in the back and a packet of wet wipes in every available pocket.
“Dennis has grandchildren,” she explains when Imani asks.
“I wasn't asking about the wipes.”
“No,” Leila says. “Sorry.”

Julian sits in the front. He has to hold a cardboard box in his lap because the passenger footwell is full of additional wet wipes. Miso stays inside the box with the flap partly open. Nobody has suggested he needs to hide; he seems to prefer being luggage to being questioned.

You are home before nine. The flat looks ordinary from the doorway. The chair you wedged under the handle is back at the kitchen table. The screw from the handle sits beside your laptop. Someone has laid the chemistry worksheet neatly on top of it, although you left it on a streetcar which crossed a river under the city.

Leila checks the rooms before letting you in. She uses a little mirror from her bag, turning it towards each corner. You want to ask how she knows what to look for. You want to go straight to bed and wake up yesterday.
There is a note on the table.
You have my face in the mirror. I'd like it back.
It is written in pencil. The letters have the careful shape of someone copying them from a sign.
Miso sniffs it, sneezes and climbs onto the windowsill.
“Don't destroy it,” Julian says.
“I wasn't going to.”
“You look like you want to.”
You put the note under an empty glass.

Imani's dad arrives while Leila is making toast. He is broad-shouldered, tired, and wearing a work jacket with a rip at the cuff. He looks first at Imani, then at Leila, then at you. His eyes stop on the dressing at your elbow.
“Car trouble?” he says.
Leila turns off the toaster.
“A situation at the building. I needed Imani to help Sam get out.”
“What situation?”
“The door wouldn't open safely.”

You can see her searching for a statement that is accurate enough to survive. You used to think grown-ups had some private source of better explanations. Watching your aunt choose each word, you begin to suspect that a lot of adulthood is deciding how much trouble the next sentence will cause.
Imani's dad doesn't like the answer. He doesn't have time to stay and dislike it properly. He tells Imani to get her bag.
She says, “I need to come back later.”
“For what?”
“Helping.”
“Helping somebody else miss school?”
“Dad.”
“Selection is tomorrow. You told me that was important.”
“It is.”
“Then eat. Sleep. And answer your phone.”
She takes the toast Leila offers and wraps it in a paper towel. At the door she looks back at you, waiting for something.
You realise you haven't thanked her.
“Thanks.”
She gives a short nod. It isn't quite the response you wanted, but you aren't sure what response you earned.
After she leaves, Julian telephones his college and says he has a family emergency. He doesn't stumble over the lie. When he catches you looking, he covers the receiver.
“My manager won't write 'trapped in another realm' on a reference.”
Leila calls your school. You hear her say medical issue, family situation, expected back Monday. The office person asks a question that makes her close her eyes.
“No. We don't have an update about Nadia.”
You leave the kitchen before she can finish.

Your room smells of the orange peel you left on the desk yesterday. The bed is unmade. A clean school shirt hangs from the wardrobe handle because Leila refuses to put away clothes you are perfectly capable of putting away yourself. Everything in the room is arranged around a person who thought they knew how Friday would go.
You sit on the bed and take off your boots. Your socks have dried stiff at the ankles.
In your phone's drafts is the last message you wrote to Mum. You open it.
Leila bought the wrong cereal again. I know you'd say it's the same cereal in a different box. It isn't. You can tell.
There is no ending to the message. You always got stuck there. How do you say goodbye to an email address when you've spent months insisting you're only saying see you later?
You delete nothing. You close the draft.

On the other side of the wall, Julian and Leila are talking quietly. You can make out your name, Voss's name, the word lower. A chair scrapes. You press your face into the pillow, angry at how tired you are.
When you wake, someone has put a glass of water by the bed. The flat is silent except for Miso snoring on your clean shirt.
It is two in the afternoon.
Your phone contains a message from Imani: Don't do the important bit without telling me.
Underneath is a second message.
Seriously.
You lie there with the phone balanced on your chest. Then you reply: Haven't found the important bit yet.
The typing indicator appears immediately.
You could start by asking.

By the time Imani returns, Leila has covered the kitchen table with paper. Hospital forms, archive printouts, pages copied from the notebook. She has weighed the corners down with tins because the radiator makes a draft she doesn't trust.
Julian has drawn a map on the back of a grocery receipt. It is not a reassuring map. Arrows lead into boxes labelled POSSIBLY STORAGE and DO NOT ASSUME STAIRS.
“I thought you worked there,” you say.
“I work in the part where we catalogue telephones.”
He turns the receipt over. On the other side, between onions and detergent, is a name written several times. Ruth Park.
“My sister,” he says before you ask. “I'm supposed to remember her wedding.”
“You forgot?”
“I traded a memory for access to an address book. I meant to give away a Wednesday afternoon. The person taking it said that was fine.”
“What happened?”
“I didn't specify which Wednesday. Or who I was with. Weddings aren't always on Saturdays.”
He folds the receipt so the name disappears.
Leila reaches for a pencil. “We're not bargaining with anyone.”
“Depends what they're asking,” Imani says.
Your aunt gives her the look she uses when a patient has found a treatment on the internet. Imani returns it without seeming especially concerned.

You open the ledger copy from Mrs. Bell's flat. Nadia's entry has two boxes: sender present and receiving witness. Voss's name appears in the second. There should be a signature underneath. Instead somebody has crossed the return line out.
Miso walks over the papers and sits beside it.
“That isn't a cancellation,” he says.
“What is it?”
“A diversion.”
Julian leans close. The pencil work is difficult to separate from the ruled line beneath it. He follows the marks with the blunt end of his pen.
“He sent her connection somewhere else.”
The kitchen feels too warm. You pull at the collar of your coat, which you haven't taken off since waking.
“Where?”
“The lower station. But the route's been renamed. We need its first designation.”
“Then we ask Voss.”
Leila shakes her head. “Adrian will tell you enough to make you do what he wants.”
“He's the only person who's offered to talk.”
The words land where you intend them to. You aren't proud of the small relief that follows.

Your aunt puts the pencil down. “He paid for the first equipment. He designed most of the line controls. Your mother needed a way to hold two incompatible signals apart, and he had spent half his working life solving exactly that kind of problem. At first it was useful.”
“And then his daughter died.”
Leila's eyes narrow. “How do you know that?”
You show her the photograph from the cupboard, which Julian brought in his box. The girl in the yellow coat stands beside a woman whose face has been cut out of the picture.
“Eva,” Leila says. “His wife left him after the funeral. Don't invent a story about that. I don't know why she left.”
Imani picks up one of the printouts. It is a donor report, neatly formatted, with Voss's full name and the date Nadia stopped signing the weekly test sheets.
“Eleven months,” she says. “Why is it starting now?”
Nobody has an answer ready.
Then Julian takes the bell diagram and turns it ninety degrees. The twelve scratches around its edge align with twelve smaller marks in Mum's circuit.
“They're holding intervals. Not months exactly. Load cycles.”
He draws a thirteenth mark. It crosses all the others.
“When the last interval closes, every waiting message tries to complete at the same time.”
You think of the boy with the bread. The woman waiting on the platform. The person wearing your face.
“How many?”
Julian doesn't write a number. He puts his pen down.
You take your phone out before anybody can tell you not to. Voss's message is still there. This time it displays a number. You press call.
He answers on the second ring.
“Sam. Is Leila with you?”
“Yes.”
“Good. I'd prefer she heard this too.”
That is an intelligent thing to say. You dislike him a little more for saying it.
“Where's my mother?”
“Alive. I spoke to her this morning.”
Leila holds out a hand. You don't give her the phone.
“Put her on.”
“I can't from here. I can show you the direct line. But I need you to come to the gallery on Harbord. Four o'clock. Public place. Bring whoever you need to feel comfortable.”
“Why not come here?”
“Because Miso will prevent you listening.”
The cat doesn't look away from the phone.
Voss continues. “You'll hear some very alarming things about me. Several are true. Ask yourself why nobody else has brought your mother home.”
The call ends.
Imani watches you set the phone down. “He's good at that.”
“I noticed.”
“Did you?”
You want to tell her you aren't stupid. Instead you look at the timetable on her screen, which she has been checking between sentences. Saturday morning. A rink address. A time in bold.
“You don't have to come.”
“I know.”
“You keep saying that.”
“Because you keep saying it like I don't.”
She takes the receipt map and puts it inside her phone case. It is a small practical act, and the argument you were preparing has nowhere sensible to go.

At the bottom of one routing sheet, a note specifies that diverted calls carry the next reserved receiving date, not the time of the speaker. You copy it because it may explain tomorrow on your phone. It does not yet explain whose voice you heard.

c09a.title: The Person in the Group Chat

beats.text: Your friend Ella messages while Julian is sorting the gallery numbers. She sends a photograph of the chemistry board, followed by a second photograph because the first is blurred.

You haven't replied to her last four messages. You meant to. At first you didn't know what to say. Then replying required explaining why you hadn't replied, and the explanation became another message you couldn't finish.
Now she writes: Your aunt said medical. You okay?
You type yes, delete it, and type: At home. Family thing. Thanks for the notes.
Three dots appear.
You don't have to do a whole update. Just send a full stop sometimes so I know you're not dead.

You stare at the screen. The word dead looks different when someone uses it carelessly. It also looks like a word a friend might use because she has no idea how to ask the careful question without sounding like everybody else.
You send a full stop.
Her reply comes immediately: Incredible. Communication.
You laugh before remembering you are supposed to be frightened. It is a small sound, but Julian looks up.
“Something useful?”
“Yes,” you say. “Not about this.”

c09a~1.title: The Person in the Group Chat

beats.text: You take the phone into the sitting room and call her. She answers with, “Oh. A voice. Didn't know yours still worked.”
“Sometimes.”

She tells you about school. Someone has moved your locker contents because the hinge broke again. Your chemistry teacher has decided to give everyone an extra week on the project, which Ella calls a personal apology from the universe. A boy you don't particularly like has been saying things about your attendance. She tells you she dealt with it, then refuses to specify how.

For several minutes you are allowed to be irritated by the correct small things. You sit on the floor beside the sofa and pick at a loose thread while she complains about the cafeteria's attempt at soup.
Then she says, “Someone rang my mum last night. Asked for you.”
Your hand stops.
“Who?”
“Didn't say. Mum thought it was school. At three in the morning, so obviously not school, but you know how people sound official and she starts finding a pen.”
“What did they ask?”
“Your full name. Whether she knew where you were.”
You get up.
“Ella. Did she tell them?”

c09a~2.title: The Person in the Group Chat

beats.text: There is a pause. “I don't think so. Why?”
You go to the kitchen door and beckon Julian. He sees your face and puts his papers down.
“I need you to ask her. Don't call the number back.”
“Sam?”
“I know it sounds strange. Please don't call it back.”
Ella goes quiet in a way that is worse than a question. You hear her walk into another room and speak to her mother. The answer comes through indistinctly. Then Ella returns.
“She said she didn't know. She told them to call your aunt.”
You close your eyes.
“Okay. That's good.”
“Why?”
Julian holds out a scrap of paper. On it he has written: If they have a voice, they try its connections.
You think of your unanswered messages. The group chat. A person asking after you because she wants you to show up in class, accidentally becoming a line the Exchange can use.
“I can't explain all of it yet,” you say. “Something happened with Mum's work. Somebody is trying to get information through people who know us.”
That is true enough to sound worse than the version involving a talking cat.

c09a~3.title: The Person in the Group Chat

beats.text: Ella says, “Do I tell somebody?”
“Your mum. My aunt. Yes.”

Leila has come in behind Julian. You pass her the phone. She gives Ella a number for Dennis, then says the calls are part of an ongoing safety problem and should not be answered. She doesn't tell Ella she imagined anything. You hear the care in that choice.
Afterwards, Ella asks for you back.
“You could've told me there was a problem.”
“I didn't know how.”
“I didn't ask for a perfect explanation.”
You sit down again. The loose thread has wrapped around one finger so tightly it has left a red line.
“I know.”
“Do you?”
You unwind the thread.
“I think I'm starting to.”

She tells you she will keep the notes. If you need to miss another week, say so. If you don't want people asking questions, say that too. She doesn't promise to make everyone behave. She does promise to send a full stop at lunch.
You agree to send one back.

c09a~4.title: The Person in the Group Chat

beats.text: When the call ends, Julian adds Ella's household to the map. He writes only the information needed to block the diverted request, then puts the rest of the page facedown.
You recognise the distinction from Mrs. Bell's letter.
“I don't want everyone I know pulled into this.”
“Then we give the line fewer ways to mistake concern for permission.”

He shows you how to mark a receiving refusal on an ordinary piece of paper, tied to a number rather than a person. Leila calls Ella's mother and talks her through it as an unusual precaution. You can hear how odd the instructions sound. You can also hear the other woman deciding to do them anyway.
For the next twenty minutes you copy the mark onto cards for the households Leila knows have received calls. It is repetitive work. Your hand gets tired. Nothing dramatic happens.
When one of the lines on Julian's map goes dark, you keep working.

effects.detail: You helped Ella’s household refuse a diverted call.

beats.text: The gallery sells landscape paintings and very expensive lamps. Through the window you can see a blue lake rendered in thick paint, with a small red canoe positioned to make the blue seem bigger. You spend a moment wondering whether the painter has ever been in a canoe before remembering that you have come to confront a man about your missing mother.
Voss is waiting at a table near the back. He gets up when you enter.
He looks ordinary. This annoys you. His coat is hung neatly on the chair. His shirt has a pale stain near one cuff. There is a loose thread on his scarf which he keeps trying to tuck out of sight.
“Sam.” He looks at Imani. “And?”
“Imani.”
“Tea?”
“No.”
She says it before you can decide whether refusing tea makes you look more suspicious than accepting it.

Leila stands behind your chair. Miso has refused to enter the gallery, which Voss notices without asking about. You can see the cat through the window, sitting beside a planter and watching a pigeon with excessive concentration.
Voss takes a small device from his bag. It looks like a dictation recorder with a brass socket fitted into its side.
“Your mother's line. One-way for now. She won't hear you.”
You look at Leila. She nods, reluctantly.
He presses a switch.

Mum is humming. Very badly. A tune you remember because she never got past the same four notes. Something clicks. She says, “No, that won't hold,” then swears softly enough that you have to lean closer.
You cover the lower half of your face with one hand.
Leila reaches for the device. Voss lets her inspect it. She listens, checks a tiny movement in the brass socket and sets it back down.
“It's live,” she says.
Mum hums the four notes again.
“Can you tell where?” you ask.
“The lower station,” Voss says. “She made herself part of the holding circuit. I have a way to relieve her.”
Leila looks at him. “With what?”
“A willing replacement.”
“No.”
“I haven't asked Sam.”
“You don't need to.”
The woman at the front of the gallery glances over. Voss lowers his voice.
“I meant myself.”
You look at him properly for the first time.
He lets the silence sit. He is very good at leaving a space you want to fill for him.
“Why haven't you?” you ask.
“The station won't accept the person who diverted its first return line. There needs to be a witness to alter that restriction. A relative of the person holding it would be strongest.”
“Strongest,” Imani repeats.
“A connected witness.”
“You could've said that.”
Voss smiles at her without showing his teeth. “Yes.”
Leila leans forward. “You told Nadia the acknowledgement controls were manual. She trusted you.”
“They were manual.”
“You fitted a bypass.”
“To make the system stable.”
“To make it ignore refusals.”
He looks down at the loose thread on his scarf. For a moment the mild expression slips.
“People say things when they're afraid.”
The room stays quiet. On the recorder Mum says a number, corrects it and starts over. You know how she sounds when she has been working too long. She is there now.
“Eva,” you say.
Voss looks up.
“The little girl. That's who you're trying to bring back.”
His hand closes around the edge of the table.
“That's private.”
“So was Mum.”
Leila puts a hand on your shoulder. You move out from under it without thinking. Voss sees that too.

He takes a photograph from his wallet. Eva stands in the raincoat, front tooth missing, holding a small snow globe. The woman cut out of the other picture is present in this one, her arm around Eva's shoulders. She looks tired and happy and not like an explanation for anything.
“She hated snow,” he says. “Until it stopped. Then she wanted it back. Every year.”
You wait.
“I heard her through one of Nadia's early tests. Just a word. My name.”
“Did she ask you to do this?”
His eyes go flat.
“Would you have ignored your mother?”
It is the wrong question, and it still works. You look towards the recorder.
Voss pushes a card across the table. On it is an address and a time: lower entrance, six p.m. He has written the time by hand.
“You can investigate without me. I expect you will. But I have access she needs. Don't let somebody else's account of me cost you another chance.”
Outside, Miso is standing with all four paws planted against the pavement.
Voss follows your gaze. “Ask him about the collar. Ask whose name keeps it closed.”
Mum's voice stops. You reach for the recorder before you can stop yourself.
Voss turns it off.
“I'll leave you to discuss it.”
He gets up, pays for four cups of tea nobody ordered, and leaves through a side door.
For a while you sit with the photograph he forgot on the table. Then Leila turns it over.
On the back, under Eva's name, is a short list of numbers. One has been crossed out and replaced. You copy all of them.
Imani notices. She says nothing until you are outside.
“You were listening,” she says.
“You sound surprised.”
“I was worried.”
It is a different answer. You keep it to yourself instead of making a joke.

choices.label: Show Imani the copied numbers now

effects.detail: You shared Voss’s extra information before using it.

choices.label: Say he gave you nothing else; keep the clue

effects.detail: You denied having Voss’s extra clue.

beats.text: Julian finds the first number from Voss's photograph in a disconnected catalogue. It refers to a room the archive no longer owns, in a building demolished before you were born.
“Helpful,” Imani says.
“The room might still be there.”
She waits for the rest of that sentence. Julian takes off his cardigan and puts it back on as if that will make the explanation easier.
“Addresses don't disappear at the same speed as buildings.”
Miso leads you through the back of a laundrette. The owner looks up from folding towels, sees Julian and says, “If you're going downstairs, bring up my trolley.”
Julian promises to try. Outside the basement door he stops you.
“I'm not promising anything else in there. I've already lost enough.”

The stairs end in a market built from shelves. High above you, light falls through a roof of catalogue cards. People move along narrow aisles with bags held close to their chests. A man is selling keys without teeth. A woman has arranged glasses of water around a notebook. Every time she turns a page, someone whispers through the glasses.
You keep your hands in your pockets.

At the centre stands a desk broad enough to eat dinner on. Behind it a man with a long, narrow face is writing in three books at once. His left hand turns a page. His right continues writing. A third pen moves without anyone holding it.
Miso sits at a respectful distance.
The man doesn't look up. “The trolley's behind the north shelves, Julian.”
“I didn't ask.”
“You were going to. And your earlier request remains under review.”
Julian's face shuts down.
You put the copied number on the desk. The third pen stops.
“A diverted address,” the man says. “Whose permission do you bring to examine it?”
“My mother's.”
“Did she give it?”
You look at the notebook. Mum wrote your name in it. She told you to find Leila. She didn't tell you to come here.
“No.”
“Then tell me whose permission you bring.”
“Mine.”
“That I can record.”

The man draws a line under your number. When he turns his head, his shadow on the shelf has a long curved beak. You remember a school project, a picture of an ibis, your mother's patient explanation that the gods had more than one form and people should stop treating the heads like a matching quiz.
“Thoth?” you ask.
“Among other ways of asking for my attention.”
“I need the address.”
“You need access to the record of its alteration. Those are different requests.”
Imani rests her hands on the edge of the desk. “What do we have to pay?”
“An account which corrects the record.”
“That's vague.”
“It becomes less vague if you stop offering me objects I have no use for.”
You hadn't offered him anything. He looks towards the notebook under your arm, and you tuck it closer before you can help yourself.
Thoth sets one of the three books in front of you. In the first column are names. In the second, brief statements. In the third, the spaces where signatures should be.
He taps a line.
NADIA MANSOUR. EXTENDED VOLUNTARY SERVICE. AUTHORITY TO DELEGATE RECEIPT.
The signature underneath resembles your mother's. It is too tidy. She never wrote the last r in Mansour properly when she was in a hurry.
“That isn't what happened,” you say.
“Then submit evidence.”

You take out the letter from Mrs. Bell's flat. The ledger copy. Mum's recording. On their own they explain pieces. Together they show who was present, who changed the route and when your mother stopped signing.
Thoth listens to the recording without expression. When Mum swears at the battery cover, the third pen makes a small mark in its book.
“You can file these,” he says. “They will be retained until the dispute is settled.”
You hold the recorder tighter. It has her voice on it. You only just got it.
Julian puts his own recorder beside yours.
“Copy,” he says. “Remember?”

You could trust the process. You could try to steal the book and run, though every aisle looks the same and the person behind the desk has been turning pages without using his hands. You could refuse the terms and try Voss's lower entrance, knowing less about what he plans.
Thoth waits. He doesn't make the decision easier by being kind.
Behind you, a trolley rolls slowly out of a side aisle and nudges Julian's ankle.
“Thank you,” Julian says stiffly.
“Ask me for something I can return,” Thoth tells him.
Julian looks down at the handle. For a moment you think he's going to argue. Instead he takes the trolley and pushes it towards the stairs.
You look back at the disputed signature. Mum's name shouldn't be sitting in a book beside a sentence she never agreed to.
You keep one hand on the recorder while you decide.

choices.label: Submit the evidence; receive a witness seal

effects.detail: You submitted evidence to challenge the false entry.

choices.label: Keep Mum’s recorder; leave without a seal

effects.detail: You kept the evidence and accepted an uncertified route.

choices.label: Try to steal the book; risk the witness’s trust

effects.detail: You tried to steal the record you wanted corrected.

beats.text: Imani taps the place where you copied the numbers. “You said there was nothing else. Next time tell me before the locked door.”
The correction doesn't make the lie disappear. Thoth rules a narrow line through it, leaving every letter legible, and attaches a reference number to the evidence.
“People will still be able to see it?” you ask.
“They need to see what was changed.”
He writes a second address beneath the first. The marks look simple until you try to copy them. One seems to belong behind another, although they're both on the same page.
Julian turns your notebook sideways.
“Write the order separately.”
You make six small numbered boxes. Thoth watches you fill them.
“Take the witness receipt,” he says. “You may challenge a delegated authority once. It will not hold the door open for you. It will make the door ask the question it was told to skip.”
You fold the receipt along its printed line. It is longer than your pocket, so you fold it twice more. Nobody says anything about the untidy result.

The address on the public card takes longer to copy than you expect. Without a witness seal, every redirected mark has to be checked against the notebook. Julian helps without claiming you have proof you chose not to submit. You write the missing receipt on a separate line so nobody can mistake the address for one.

On the way out, Imani buys a bottle of water from the laundrette. Ordinary water, from an ordinary fridge, with an ordinary price she objects to before paying it. Julian helps carry the trolley up the stairs. The owner says, “Finally,” and gives him a packet of biscuits.

You sit on the laundrette's front step, passing the biscuits between you. It is nearly six. The sky has the flat purple colour it gets before snow, and the bus shelter across the road is crowded with people trying not to touch.
Julian takes one biscuit, then breaks it and puts half back.
“Ruth doesn't know,” he says.
You turn towards him. He keeps looking at the road.
“About the wedding. I let her think I was drunk. The photographer sent me the pictures. I know where everyone stood. I can describe the cake.”
“Doesn't that help?”
“It makes me better at lying about it.”
The laundrette door opens behind you. Warm air and the smell of soap spill over the steps. A woman carries a bag past you without looking down.
Imani asks, “What did you need the address book for?”
Julian rubs the biscuit crumbs off his hand.
“Nadia. After she disappeared. I thought I could find her before anybody noticed how much I didn't know.”
You hadn't expected that. You thought he would say a rare book, or a promotion, or a door he shouldn't have tried. Something that would make the price easier to judge.
“I didn't know you,” he adds. “It wasn't for you.”
“Okay.”
“She took me seriously. At work. That's all.”
He says that's all in a tone that makes Imani stop asking questions.

Miso is crouched under the step, watching a delivery cyclist fix a dropped chain. His collar has appeared around his neck. You haven't seen it before. Thin black leather, too tight at the throat, with a brass plate tucked under the fur.
You remember what Voss said.
“Whose name keeps it closed?”
The cat goes still.
Julian looks up sharply. “Don't.”
“Voss told me to ask.”
“Voss tells everybody something true when he wants them to stop noticing the rest.”
Miso stands and walks towards the alley. You get up after him.
“I wasn't—”
He moves faster. You follow him around the corner, leaving Imani and Julian on the step.
At the end of the alley, he turns.
“Yes,” he says. “I worked for him.”
“Doing what?”
“Opening doors. Carrying messages. Finding people he said were lost.”
“My mother?”
The question hangs there long enough to answer itself.
You sit back on a low wall. Your elbow throbs where the dressing pulls against the cut.
“You took her there.”
“She asked me to.”
“Did she know you worked for him?”
“No.”
A rubbish bag shifts in the wind. Miso watches it instead of you.
You have to put your hands somewhere. You push them under your arms.
“You could have told me.”
“I could.”
“Everyone keeps saying that after.”
He raises his head. Under the brass plate, his fur has worn away in a narrow strip.
“I don't get to tell every truth I know,” he says. “I can tell you this one because you brought it out of his mouth and put it into yours. Ask me something else about him and see what happens.”
You don't. You aren't willing to test the collar by hurting him just to see whether he's honest.
Imani appears at the corner. She stops when she sees your faces.
“Julian's got a message from Leila. Bell's getting worse. She says if we're using that address, we go now.”

Miso walks past her without speaking. You wait until he has gone, then show Imani the photograph you copied at the gallery. The list of numbers on the back. The part you hadn't told anybody about because you wanted to be the person with something useful.

She studies the page. Then she looks at you. “You said there wasn't anything else.” You start to explain about checking it. She gives the notebook back carefully. “Tell me what I'm walking into before I'm already there.”

She compares the page with the copy she made at the gallery. “Same sequence,” she says. “Good. We can stop checking one another's handwriting.” She hands the notebook back with the relevant page still open.
You put the page where everyone can see it when you return to the step.
The return address does not open on the first attempt. Julian checks your copied marks against the witness receipt, then against the number on Voss's photograph.
“He's changed the route again.”
“Can he stop us?”
“He can make the line take a different way.”
Miso sniffs the bottom of the wall. Water has begun to seep through a crack in the skirting board. It pools around his paws and reflects a ceiling the exchange room doesn't have.
“Back,” he says.
Julian grabs the equipment box. Imani takes your sleeve. The water rises in a sheet, climbing away from the floor until it stands between you and the booths.
On the other side, the reflected ceiling becomes a long throat.
You make a sound you won't later describe as a scream. Imani pulls you behind the desk as the water collapses where you were standing. It strikes the floor hard enough to split a tile.
Miso is already on a shelf. His ears are flat. Julian has the notebook open with one hand and is trying to protect the paper with the other.
“What is that?” you ask.
“A bad route,” he says. “Very bad.”

A shape gathers inside the water, narrow at the front, thickening along the floor. It moves like a snake, except the surface keeps showing things behind you. Your kitchen. A hospital corridor. The underside of Mum's table.

You remember pictures of the great serpent opposing the sun's nightly passage. The thing on the floor is much smaller, assembled out of borrowed reflections and a bad instruction. That does not make its approach feel manageable.
Julian finds a note in Mum's manual.
“It's following the strongest return signal.”
All three of you look at your phone.
You turn it off. The water keeps coming.
“Not the power,” Julian says. “The claim.”
The blue notebook is warm under your arm. You take it out and the leading edge turns towards it.
Mum's address. Your connection to her. The thing isn't choosing you because you're important. It is taking the shortest available route.
You put the notebook on the desk and step away. The water follows it, gathering against the wooden legs.
Imani looks at the high shelf near the wall. “Can it climb?”
As if answering, the water begins to climb.
Julian passes you chalk. “Hold the connection between it and the address. Don't try to hold all the water.”
You kneel behind the desk. The floor is wet. The first line dissolves before you finish it.
“Paper,” you say.

Imani tears a page from the back of an old catalogue and puts it on a dry part of the desk. You draw the mark there. It is harder with your hands shaking. You close the circle and give it a definite subject: route to address, not address to person.
The rising water pauses.
