Miso jumps to the top of the wall, where a pipe passes through a hole larger than it needs to be. He scratches at the plaster. On the other side, a narrow staircase appears, leading down past the telephone booths.
“Empty channel,” he says. “Can you send it there?”
“Can it hurt someone?” you ask.
“Not if we close it before the next arrival.”
That is not a completely reassuring answer. You think of the boy with the bread and the platforms where people wait. You don't want to push a danger out of sight and call it solved.
Julian studies the address on the notebook.
“We can use an unassigned return. No receiver. Then close both ends.”
“How?”

He shows you the open stroke on the temporary hold, then turns the page so you can see how the route should finish. You have to move the mark, not break it. If you erase the wrong side, the water will return to the strongest signal. You.

Imani puts the notebook inside the equipment box and slides the box towards the staircase. The water turns. You move the chalk line a little at a time, opening one end only after the next has been drawn.
Your hand cramps. The water trembles. You tell Imani to stop moving and wait until you can feel your fingers again.
She waits. It matters more than any encouragement she could have shouted.
At the staircase, the route narrows to a stream. The rest of the room drains into it with a sound like a bathtub emptying through a wall.
Julian counts down from three. You close the far end. He closes the near one.
The water vanishes.
For a moment nobody moves. Then the desk collapses, one leg giving way where the first impact cracked it. The notebook slides out of the box and lands at your feet, dry except along one corner.

Imani sits down on a chair that has survived and bends over her knees. Julian wipes the floor with a towel so he can examine the broken route without stepping in it. Miso climbs down from the wall, misses the last shelf and pretends he meant to land that loudly.
You pick up the notebook.
In the margin beside the return address, Mum has written a small instruction you hadn't understood before: Do not confuse connection with appetite.
You add your own note underneath.
Wet floors. Bring paper.
It isn't elegant. You think she will know what you mean.
The green door appears in the wall where you first tried the address. Through its wire-glass window, a woman sits at a table.
You stand up so fast the chair behind you falls over.

The address opens a door in the wall of the exchange room. You know the wall was blank because you helped Julian carry a shelving unit away from it. Now it has a green door with a brass number and a wire-glass window.
Behind the glass, your mother is sitting at a table.

For several seconds you don't move. She looks thinner. Her hair is cut unevenly above her shoulders, with one piece tucked behind an ear. There is a mug near her elbow. She keeps reaching for it and putting it down again without drinking.
You say, “Mum,” but there is no sound. Your mouth has done the shape and forgotten the rest.
Imani puts a hand against your back.
You try again.
Mum looks up.

Her chair falls over when she stands. You see her take two steps towards the door, then stop as a cable stretched across the table pulls tight. Her right hand is wrapped around it. The skin across her fingers is red and raw.
“Sam?”

You nod, then realise how absurd that is. She can see your face. You should say something, tell her you brought help, tell her Leila is waiting, tell her you didn't throw away the blue mug when its handle broke.
What comes out is, “I did my homework.”
Mum puts her free hand over her mouth. For a moment she looks like she might laugh. Then she starts crying, silently, with her eyes still fixed on you.
Julian opens the door just far enough to pass a piece of chalk through. He keeps one foot against the bottom.
“There's a load on the threshold,” he says. “We need something to hold it.”

You kneel and draw the mark. Your first circle comes out lopsided. You rub it away with your sleeve and start again. Forty-one seconds in the exchange room wasn't enough. You need longer now. You close the last line and tell the chalk exactly which connection you intend to hold: door, frame, this side, that side.
The green paint goes pale. Julian pushes. The gap widens.
Imani braces her stick against the wall and slides through first. You follow her into a room that smells of dust and hot wiring.
Mum is close enough to touch.
You don't run at her. You think you might break something if you do. You walk carefully around a chair and take her free hand.
It is warm. There is a hard patch on the side of her middle finger where she always held a pen. You press your thumb against it, needing proof more precise than her face.
She pulls you against her shoulder.
“Your hair,” she says.
“Leila cut it.”
“I can tell.”
You make a sound that hurts your throat. Her free arm tightens around you. You would like the next minute to be uncomplicated. You would like at least that much.
The cable jerks. Mum gasps and lets you go.
Julian is standing beside the table, reading the labels on a panel. “We can relieve the hand control. Where's the second reader?”
“Disconnected.”
“Where?”
“Adrian took it out.”
Imani holds the door. “We have six minutes.”
You look at Mum's hand. The cable passes through a loop of brass fitted around her wrist. It isn't tied. The loop has closed into itself.
“Can we cut it?”
“No.”
She says it too quickly, then catches herself.
“Listen. It's carrying people. Messages with the connections still attached. If we cut indiscriminately, the damage travels back to the living end.”
“Then let go.”
“I did. Once.”
The room becomes quiet except for a relay clicking under the table.
Mum points to a row of labels. Three are blank.
“I didn't know who they belonged to until they went blank.”
You want to argue that she couldn't know, that this isn't her fault. But you don't know enough yet to tell her what belongs to her and what doesn't. You hold her free hand instead.
Julian finds a second connector behind the panel. “It's still here. He removed the receiver, not the socket.”
He reaches in.
Miso says, “Wait.”
The room lights go out.
For a second you can hear breathing from everywhere, too many people sharing too little air. Then a child's voice speaks through the wall.
“Dad says you can't take her yet.”
Imani pulls you backwards as the table shifts. One leg sinks through the floor. Mum reaches for you with her free hand, misses, catches your coat.
The seam by the bird patch tears.
Miso leaps onto the panel. His claws scrape metal. Julian is trying to pull the connector free, but his hand has gone rigid. You see the skin on his wrist turning grey.
There is time to reach one of them before the door closes. Mum is standing. Julian isn't moving. Imani's stick has begun to bend against the frame.

choices.label: Pull Julian free; leave the spare connector

effects.detail: You chose him over a useful component.
You pulled Julian free at the first rescue.

choices.label: Take the connector while Imani rescues Julian

effects.detail: You chose the component while Imani pulled him free.

beats.text: Leila doesn't ask whether you found Nadia. She sees you carrying Julian and opens the fire door wider.

You sit him in a chair. His hand is grey to the wrist, the fingers stiff and curled. Imani puts the broken hockey stick against the wall. The blade has separated along one layer, leaving a thin splinter that she keeps touching with her thumb.
Leila cuts Julian's sleeve away.
“Can you feel that?”
“Yes.”
“This?”
“No.”
She asks the same questions twice more, then turns to Miso.
“What travelled up the connection?”
“Claim. Not damage. Yet.”
“Can you reverse it?”
“Not while it has his agreement.”
Julian looks up. “I didn't agree.”
Miso's tail moves sharply once. “You touched the free connector.”
“I was trying to help.”
“Nobody asked why.”
Leila looks at the cat. He stops talking.

You stand near the coffee stain, which someone has put a wet-floor sign over instead of cleaning. You keep seeing Mum reach for you. Her hand closing on the coat. The patch tearing. You could have held on longer. You know the door was closing. You could still have tried.
Leila finishes wrapping Julian's hand in loose cloth, then comes to you.
“Let me see the elbow.”
“It doesn't matter.”
“Let me see it anyway.”
You push up your sleeve. The dressing has soaked through.
She looks at the cut and goes still in the careful way that means she is trying not to react. Then she takes your arm gently and washes it.
“She was there,” you say.
“I know.”
“You don't. You weren't—”
“I know she was there. I don't know what it was like. Tell me.”
You look at the top of her head. Her hair is going grey near the parting. You haven't noticed that before, though it must have been happening in the same flat you live in.
“She asked about my hair.”

Leila presses her lips together. You try to explain the cable, the panel, the part of Mum's hand you held. None of it comes in the right order. Leila doesn't correct you. When she tapes the clean dressing down, her fingers are shaking.
You say, “Why didn't she call?”
The question has been waiting for eleven months. Now that you know she's alive, it feels harder to ask.
Miso answers from beside Julian's chair.
“Every outside call has a cost. The first ones went to people Adrian chose. After she realised, she stopped trying.”
“Except mine.”
“You don't know who made yours.”
You look at the phone in your hand. Friday, nine forty-seven p.m. The unknown call is listed at two thirteen. Tomorrow's date has returned beside it.
Julian has stopped moving his grey fingers.
“The return line isn't just misdirected,” he says. “It's carrying an instruction. You can't pull her out while that instruction still names her as the receiver.”
“So change the name.”
“To who?”
The room goes quiet.

You hear the idea before you admit it's yours. Your name. Your hand on the cable. Mum walking out. There must be a way to stand where she is until somebody fixes it properly. You could learn enough. You've already learned more today than you thought possible.
Leila looks at you.
“No.”
“I didn't say anything.”
“You didn't have to.”
Imani gets up to leave. You turn towards her, suddenly afraid she has had enough. She lifts her damaged stick.
“I have to be at the rink at ten. My dad's taking me. If I don't sleep now I might as well not go.”
You almost ask how she can think about hockey. Then you see the tape worn smooth where her glove rests, the careful way she avoids putting weight on the damaged blade.
“Can you use another one?”
“I've got an older one.”
“I'm sorry.”
“I know.”
She puts on her coat. At the door she says, “You should come. Not for the hockey. Just get out of here for an hour.”
You look towards the bell cupboard.
“It won't all happen because you sat down,” she says.
After she leaves, Leila makes you eat soup from a paper cup. It is too hot. You drink it anyway, standing near Julian while he uses his good hand to redraw the connector he couldn't reach.
At the bottom of the drawing, beside the receiver slot, he writes one word.
CONSENT.
Then he crosses it out and writes: REMOVAL OF REFUSAL.
You fold the page carefully. This time you know which question to bring back.

c15.title: The Wrong End of the Rink

beats.text: You wake to somebody knocking on a metal door and spend several seconds trying to remember which side you're on.

Then you recognise the annex storeroom. Leila has made a bed from two coats and a camping mat Dennis found in his car. Julian is asleep in the chair, his bandaged hand supported by a rolled towel. Miso occupies the warm patch under the radiator.
The knocking is Dennis. He has brought porridge, four plastic spoons and a large piece of paper on which he has written EMERGENCY CONTACTS in capital letters.
“Somebody ought to know where everybody is,” he says.
You eat the porridge. It tastes of the inside of the cardboard tub. When you check your phone, Imani has sent the rink address with no explanation.
Leila sees you put your boots on.
“Where?”
“Rink.”
She looks at the clock, then at the bell cupboard. The holding mark has been renewed so many times that white dust covers the hinges.
“Take your phone.”
“I was planning to.”
“And don't—”
She stops. You wait.
“Tell me when you get there.”
You nod. It is a smaller request. You can manage it.

c15~1.title: The Wrong End of the Rink

beats.text: The rink smells of old rubber and cold air. Parents lean against the barrier holding paper cups. Someone is arguing about a helmet. Through the glass, skaters move between cones while a coach points at something you can't identify.

Imani is near the goal, wearing a helmet with a white scratch across the front. You hadn't realised how much equipment she needs to stand there. Her gloves look enormous. The substitute stick is dark green, with tape peeling from the shaft.
Her dad spots you and lifts his chin in greeting.
“Your aunt get the car sorted?”
“Mostly.”
“Good.”
He watches Imani stop a shot, then says, “She nervous?”
“I don't know.”
“Won't tell me.”
You have no advice for him. He seems content not to receive any.

For twenty minutes nothing supernatural happens. Nobody's reflection moves incorrectly. The scoreboard displays a sensible number. A child drops a mitten down the gap behind a bench and becomes much more upset than the situation seems to warrant, until you remember you don't know what else happened to them today.

c15~2.title: The Wrong End of the Rink

beats.text: Imani misses a shot. Her dad shifts his weight. You glance at him, but he is smiling slightly.
“Too far out,” he says, to himself.
You watch the next shot closely enough to see what he means. The puck goes left, Imani moves, the glove closes. Her dad taps the barrier with two fingers. She doesn't look over.
Your phone vibrates.
Julian: Found a maintenance entry. Maybe a way around the witness circuit. Need original operator manual.
A second message follows.
Might be in the flat. Don't go without Leila.
You look at the rink doors. You could leave now and be at the flat before the session ends. You know where Mum kept her manuals. Imani wouldn't notice until she came off the ice.
On the far side of the glass, she looks towards the benches. Her helmet turns just enough for you to know she's seen you.

effects.detail: You stayed to watch the session when the archive called.
You made time for Imani’s life outside the rescue.

choices.label: Leave to find the manual; tell her afterwards

effects.detail: You left the rink without telling her directly.

beats.text: The flat is colder than you remember. Leila goes straight to the radiator and turns the valve, then checks the mirror by the front door before allowing anyone to take off a coat.
Imani goes to the kitchen. Julian checks the window latch. Miso stays on the threshold, making a point of waiting until you look at him.
“You're coming in,” you say.
He steps over without answering.

Mum's manuals are on the bottom shelf in the sitting room. You used to build little walls around them with your schoolbooks because she complained when you stacked anything heavy on top. Most are ordinary repair guides, full of parts diagrams and warnings about electricity. The one you need has no title on its spine.
Inside, someone has written a list of names. You recognise Nadia, Adrian, Celia. The fourth is Leila's.
You bring the book into the kitchen.
Your aunt has filled the kettle. She turns it off before it boils.
“I witnessed the first tests,” she says.
“Of course you did.”
She looks at the open page instead of defending herself.
“There were people at the hospital who died before someone could get there. Nadia wanted to know whether something could be done about that.”
“You helped.”
“Yes.”
“Did they know?”
“Some did. We asked. We wrote it down. Not everybody said yes.”
You turn the page. Beside several names, in your aunt's compact handwriting, is the word declined. No explanation. No attempt to talk them round.
“What happened to the noes?”
“Nothing. That was the point.”
Julian sets his bandaged hand on the table. Leila looks at it and closes her eyes briefly.
“Adrian wanted the line to stay open after a refusal. He said someone might change their mind. Nadia said they could make a new call.”
“And you?”
“I thought a delay could be harmless if nobody received anything until they agreed.”
You wait. She rubs one thumb against the other.
“I signed off on a delay. I didn't ask enough about what he did with it.”
Miso sits beneath the chair nearest her. He doesn't look comfortable.

You keep turning pages. The manual shows two identical sockets facing each other. One is labelled CALL. The other is labelled RECEIVE. In between, a line returns to the caller before the circuit closes.
The bypass crosses that line.
Julian leans over your shoulder.
“It never asks again. It records the first contact as continuing authority.”
Your aunt nods. “When Nadia found out, she tried to shut it down from inside. She thought she could put the original check back.”
“She told you?”
“She told me after she went.”
The kettle clicks as it cools. Nobody moves towards it.
“I got one call,” Leila says. “She said she was handling it. She sounded annoyed with herself. I was annoyed with her too. I told her to stop trying to fix everything alone.”
“What did she say?”
“She asked me to stay with you until she got back.”
You look down at the list of declined names. Your aunt has made the same mistake as your mother: turning a request into an arrangement that keeps lasting because nobody knows how to end it.
“You should've told me,” you say.
“I should have told you enough to understand why I didn't have an answer.”
“That's a very careful sentence.”
“Yes.”
You put the manual down. Your hands have started trembling, not dramatically, just enough to make the paper rustle. You hate it. You hold the edge of the table until it stops.
Imani opens a cupboard, finds mugs and lines four of them beside the kettle. She doesn't ask whether anyone wants tea. The practical interruption gives you somewhere to put your eyes.
Julian studies the socket diagram.
“We need another reader. Independent. Not a replacement body.”
Miso says, “Adrian still has the original.”
You look at him.
He lowers his head and scratches at the collar. The brass plate makes a thin sound against his claws.
“I can tell you where he stores things,” he says. “I can't promise the things are there.”
Leila turns a page back and points to a smaller diagram you nearly missed. It shows how to release a connection without cutting through it. Two marks, one inside the other, followed by an open end.
“I'm going to teach you this,” she says. “Then you're going to teach it back to me before you try it on anything.”
You sit down. She gives you a scrap of paper and draws the first line slowly.

It takes almost an hour. You get impatient twice. She gets impatient once and apologises before you have to point it out. Imani practises with a piece of string. Julian records the sequence in words as well as pictures.
Miso watches from the chair. When the string loosens without breaking, he looks away.
You keep the scrap of paper. On the back, under the grocery list already written there, you put the date and the word release.
Julian finds the box while searching for a spare socket. It sits behind two old lamps in a cupboard your mother told you contained nothing interesting.
Inside are six little clay figures, each about the length of your thumb. They have rough bodies, plain faces and a mark on the back. You take one out. It is surprisingly heavy.
“Shabti?” you ask.
“Modern practice models,” Julian says. “Nadia made them. Don't start thinking the museum lends out ancient funerary equipment.”

There are notes under the tissue. Mum has drawn a picture of a worker figure holding a basket, then written several pages about why telling a created thing to perform an endless task is a poor starting point for any safe experiment.
Her own models are supposed to carry a defined load from one point to another and stop when the task is complete.
Imani turns a figure over.
“So little delivery people.”
“Little load markers,” Julian says.
“That's less fun.”
You line them up on the table. The figures do not look particularly interested in either description.

Mum's notes describe a way to divide a connection among several temporary holders. It is not enough for the lower station's load. It might be enough to steady a reader while somebody changes a setting.

Julian gets the second practice handset. You draw the required marks. Imani positions the little figures along the cable, using a ruler because she has decided guessing is how everybody got into trouble.
The first figure moves when you complete the circuit.
Not much. It lifts one foot, puts it down and tips over.
Imani catches it.
“Strong start.”
Julian takes it from her and checks the mark. “The subject's wrong. You're asking it to hold the entire call, not one defined segment.”
You alter the line. This time the figure stands with both feet on the table. The second follows it. Then the third.
For a few seconds, the handset cable hangs in a precise curve between them without touching the wood.
You grin before you can help it.
Then the fourth figure turns towards you.
“Further instruction?” it asks in your own voice.
You stop grinning.
Julian reaches for the circuit. Imani puts one hand above it without touching.
“Ask it to stop first.”
You do. The figure remains standing.
“Further instruction?”
The fifth figure turns. Then the sixth.

Your drawing has a closed return at the far end. You copied it from an early page in Mum's notes, before the correction on the next sheet. The figures are not ignoring you. The circuit has no recognised completion.
They begin passing the little load back to the first one.
The cable tightens around the ruler. Imani moves her hand away. A crack appears in one clay shoulder.
You want to snatch the figure up. Julian catches your wrist.
“Connection,” he says. “Not the body.”
You take the paper Leila taught you from your pocket. The release sequence is simple enough to remember until you need it. You set it beside the practice mark and copy the first outer line.
The little figures turn with you, all six faces following the chalk.
“Further instruction?”
“End this task,” you say. “No replacement task. No further holding.”
The outer mark opens.
One figure sits down. Then another. The cable falls onto the table. The last figure says your name once, quietly, and becomes clay again.
Nobody speaks for a while.
You pick up the one with the cracked shoulder. Mum's thumbprint is visible near its base. You rub a finger over it and put the figure back in the box.
Julian writes the corrected sequence in large letters. Imani puts a strip of blue tape on the page you missed.
Leila comes in from the sitting room and looks at the table.
“What did you learn?”
You could say the figures work. It would be true. You could also omit the part where they nearly broke while following exactly what you asked.
Instead you show her both pages.
She studies them, then the cracked clay.
“Nadia should have marked this better.”
You are ready to defend Mum. Then you remember you were the one standing here when the cable tightened.
“Yes,” you say.
Leila sits down and helps you label every earlier version. She doesn't lecture. She makes you check each page against the next. It takes another half-hour.

At the end, you pack three unbroken figures in a padded tin. They aren't a solution to the whole station. They are a tool for a defined job. You write the exact job on a card and put it in the tin with them.
Imani reads it before you close the lid.
“Good,” she says. “They get to go home when they're done.”

choices.label: Pack the tested clay models for a defined task

effects.detail: You tested and corrected Nadia’s clay load holders.

choices.label: Leave the models; keep the release notes

beats.text: Miso lets you examine the collar after everyone else has left the kitchen. That seems important. He waits until Leila is carrying the mugs away, then jumps onto the table and sits with his head turned so the brass plate faces you.
You don't touch it immediately.
“What happens if I ask the wrong thing?”
“Usually I can't answer. Sometimes I can, and regret it.”
“Who put it on?”
“Adrian.”
“What does it do?”
“Keeps me available.”
You look towards the manual on the table.
“The same system.”
“Older version. He practised.”
Miso says it flatly. He has stopped doing anything with his tail.
The brass plate is scratched almost smooth. Under the scratches, a name has been pressed into the metal. You can read the first mark, but the rest seem to turn away when you look directly at them.
“Is that your name?”
“A name I gave him. I was looking for somewhere warm. He had a house with a boiler room. He asked if I would help keep the doors in order.”
“What kind of doors?”
“Ordinary ones, then less ordinary ones. I should have asked better.”
“You're a cat.”
“Yes.”
You wait for a joke. He doesn't provide one.
“Are you Bast?”
“No.” His ears flatten. “She has more important complaints.”
“Then what are you?”
“A guardian. Small place. Small work. Places collect habits. Some of us learn how to hold them.”
“The flat?”
“Not originally.”
He looks at the window. A pigeon lands outside, inspects the sill and leaves. His head follows it before he remembers to be upset.
“Why did you take Mum to him?”
“I knew she could help with the doors. I didn't know he meant to close one behind her.”
You want him to say he fought, that he tried to warn her, that he spent eleven months planning to fix it. You don't want a simple statement that leaves you to work out what to feel.
“Did you try to stop him afterwards?”
“Yes.”
“How?”
He turns so you can see the bare strip beneath the collar. There are healed scratches on his skin, close together.
You sit back.
“I need to know where his workshop is,” you say.
“Then ask me where the equipment was stored when I last saw it. Don't ask where he is now. The wording matters.”

You ask carefully. He gives you an address near the waterfront, then specifies a side entrance and a set of internal stairs. Julian writes it down from the doorway. Neither of you had heard him return.
Miso watches the pen move. “Second floor. Room with no windows. There was a yellow cupboard.”
“What opened it?” Julian asks.
The collar tightens. You see Miso's shoulders rise before he can stop them.
“Stop,” you say.
Julian puts the pen down. “Sorry.”

You look at the release diagram. Leila has made you repeat it until you can draw it without looking. The collar is a connection. It carries an agreement. If you can hold both ends and allow a refusal—
Miso steps back as your hand moves.
“Ask.”
You stop.
“Can I try to loosen it?”
He looks at the chalk. Then at you.
“Not off. Not yet. If it breaks, he knows where I am. Loosen it enough that I can choose where to stand.”
You draw on the table around his paws. The marks need a definite subject. You say his name, Miso, and feel the circle lose its shape.
“That's what we call you,” you say. “It doesn't work.”
“It works for me.”

You try again. This time you think about the cat sitting in front of you, the yoghurt lid, the cold fire escape, his decision to come when your door opened. The collar is attached to a name Voss has kept. You are trying to make room for a name its wearer still uses.
The chalk lifts a fraction from the table.
Miso closes his eyes. He breathes out. The collar loosens enough to leave a narrow gap.
Your hands cramp. Julian puts a glass of water within reach but doesn't touch you. You hold the line for twelve seconds, then twenty. At thirty, Miso steps out of the circle.
The collar stays on. It is visibly looser.
He sits on the far end of the table, trying to look as if nothing has happened. You drink the water with both hands.
“Did it help?” you ask.
“Yes.”
“Good.”
Leila comes back and sees the chalk marks. She begins to speak, then looks at Miso and closes her mouth.
You clean the table before she can ask. Miso follows the cloth with one paw, a movement so ordinary you almost miss it.
At the kitchen door he stops.
“The yellow cupboard has a false back,” he tells Julian. “He changed the lock. Not the wall.”
Then he goes to sit on your clean school shirt.

effects.detail: You asked before loosening Miso’s collar.

beats.text: By late afternoon, every map on the table points towards the lake. You begin to suspect maps prefer problems which can be solved by drawing a line downwards.

Julian marks Voss's workshop, the annex and the old exchange room in different colours. Leila adds places where she has received calls since Nadia disappeared. A hospital car park. A supermarket. The bus stop outside the flat. None is on the line Julian drew.
“People,” Imani says.
He looks up.
“You're joining buildings. He connects people.”

She takes the pencil and writes names beside the points. At the hospital car park, Leila had been waiting for a colleague whose husband was dying. At the supermarket she'd met an elderly neighbour who asked after Nadia. At the bus stop, she'd been speaking to you.
The second set of lines makes an untidy knot.
Miso stands at the window. “He's getting impatient.”
The glass reflects an extra building on the opposite side of the road. It has too many windows and no ground-floor door. As you watch, a light comes on in each window, one at a time.
Your phone displays nine missed calls. It hasn't rung.
The first is from Mum. The second is from a schoolfriend you haven't spoken to properly since September. The third has no name. You don't open any of them.
Julian checks his own screen. The date has changed to Sunday.
“He's speeding the cycles.”
“Can he do that?” Imani asks.
“Apparently.”

Leila goes to the bell cupboard. She has moved it into the flat inside a locked metal case, because she finally admitted that trying to protect you from a different building was mostly protecting herself from seeing what you were doing. The chalk marks on the case are warmer than the wall around them.
“We still have time,” she says. “But less room for guessing.”
You look at the copied numbers from Voss's photograph. One is a storage reference. One is an incoming line. The crossed-out one refers to a test Nadia performed before the bypass went in.
“If we find that recording, we can show what the system was supposed to ask.”
Julian nods. “And use it to calibrate the second reader.”

The reader is in the workshop. The recording is indexed under Eva's name. For the first time, you have a plan with two tasks that can be described without saying something vague about saving everybody.
Then Dennis phones Leila. You can hear him through the receiver.
“The back room's started getting calls.”
“What back room?”
“All of them.”
Leila closes her eyes. When she opens them, she is looking at the metal case.
“I have to go back.”
You start to object. She raises one hand, then lowers it again.

“I am asking you to hear the plan before arguing. Dennis can hold the case if I show him how. I can stop the annex lines from answering automatically. Then I come to the workshop. I won't enter the other side without telling you.”
“You promise?”
“Yes.”

You check the equipment bag. Chalk, manual, notebook, ordinary torch, ordinary first-aid supplies, the feather, water. Imani adds a roll of tape and a screwdriver from her dad's tool bag. She has told him she is helping Leila move storage equipment. He told her to return the screwdriver.
Julian brings the recorder and a pair of rubber gloves. His injured hand can move at the wrist now, though the fingers remain grey.

On the street, snow has begun to fall. People hunch into their coats. At a crossing, the signal takes so long to change that a man beside you sighs and gives up waiting. He walks to the next corner instead. You watch him go, briefly jealous of a problem with another corner available.
Imani catches you looking at your phone.
“You can say you're scared without making it the whole plan.”
“I wasn't going to say it.”
“I noticed.”
You put the phone away.

At the streetcar stop, an advertisement shows a family laughing around a kitchen table. You have always disliked photographs of families laughing around kitchen tables. Nobody ever looks as if they're laughing at something specific. Now the printed mother turns her head and looks at you.
The rest of the family keep smiling in the wrong direction.
Miso presses against your boot. You move between him and the shelter glass.
“You don't have to do that,” he says.
“I know.”
The printed mother puts a hand against the inside of the advertisement. Her fingers leave marks on the glass.
Imani takes a step away. “How long until our streetcar?”
“Three minutes.”
“Let's walk.”
Nobody argues.
You find Eva's mother's address in a letter attached to the old equipment inventory. The letter asks the archive to stop forwarding calls to her number. It is dated three weeks after Eva died.
Leila reads it without saying anything for a long time.
“I didn't know about this.”
“Would it have changed anything?” you ask.
She looks at you. “It should have.”

You go because Julian needs to establish which call was the first, and because the archive record lists Mara Voss as a receiving witness. You do not go because a grieving woman owes you an explanation. You repeat that distinction to yourself on the pavement outside her building, trying to make sure it is more than a sentence that lets you knock.
Imani comes with you. Julian waits in a café across the road with the equipment. Miso has refused to leave the annex's radiator, where he is recovering from the loosened collar.
Mara answers through the intercom. You give Nadia's name and say there may be a record she can correct. The silence lasts long enough that you start preparing to leave.
Then the door buzzes.
Her flat has plants on the windowsill and a bicycle leaning against the hall wall. It is not arranged around Eva's absence in a way you can read. You are ashamed of having looked for that.
She lets you stand inside the doorway but does not offer chairs.
“Adrian sent you?”
“No.”
“Does he know you're here?”
“No.”
She studies you. There is a family resemblance you didn't notice in the photograph: Eva's eyebrows, the way she held one shoulder slightly higher than the other.
You show her the inventory letter. Mara reads it and hands it back.
“I asked them to disconnect it.”
“They didn't.”
“I worked that out.”
You start to explain what the line has become. She holds up one hand.
“I don't want a demonstration.”
“We haven't brought one.”
“Good.”
Imani gives her the copied witness entry. It is a better choice than offering another story about the dead. Mara checks the date.
“That wasn't when she called.”

She goes to a drawer and brings back a calendar. Not the one Voss kept. This one has appointments, bills, ordinary things continuing after the funeral. She finds a note written between a dentist appointment and a reminder to return a library book.
“Here. I wrote it down because I thought I was losing my mind.”
The date is earlier than the archive entry by four days.
Julian's notes come back to you. First contact treated as continuing authority. Reopened channels counted as the same call. Voss changed not just the destination but the point where the record began.
“Can we copy that date?”
Mara nods. You write only the date and the source of the correction. When you hand the calendar back, she looks relieved enough that you understand she expected you to ask for the whole page.
“Did she say anything else?” you ask, then stop. “You don't have to tell us.”
Mara leans against the wall.
“She told me where she put a note. That's all I needed.”
You wait.
“Adrian wanted another conversation. Then a longer one. Then proof the next voice was her. There was always something else the call needed to do before he could let it end.”
She doesn't say whether she forgave him. You don't ask.
“My mum's trapped in his system,” you say.
Mara looks towards the window. On the sill, a plant has grown against the glass and bent back towards the room.
“I know she's missing.”
“We found her.”
Her attention returns to you at once.
“Alive?”
“Yes.”
She closes her eyes. Not in disbelief. As if she has been holding a fact in one place and must now move it without dropping everything around it.
“Tell her I'm sorry I didn't call sooner.”
“You didn't do this.”
Mara opens her eyes.
“You don't know what I did or didn't do.”
The correction is fair. You had offered her the comfortable sentence because it was easier than hearing another difficult account.
You nod. “I'll tell her.”
At the door, Mara asks for Leila's number. You give it only after calling your aunt to ask. The small delay feels awkward. Mara waits without objection.
Outside, Imani walks half a block before speaking.
“You nearly said it.”
“What?”
“That she'd helped us, so now she had to help again.”
“I didn't.”
“No. You stopped.”

Across the road, Julian has ordered one tea and been given a pot large enough for four people. He has spent the waiting time drawing the receiving circuit on a napkin, which the server has tactfully avoided clearing.
You show him the corrected date. He compares it with the two inventory references, then draws a line beneath the original call.
“This is the one. Eva's voice, not a later imitation.”
Imani pours the remaining tea into two cups. It is almost cold. You drink it anyway.
Through the café window, Mara cycles past wearing a bright green helmet. She doesn't see you. She is going somewhere that has nothing to do with your investigation.
You watch her turn the corner, then look back at the number Julian has circled.

The recording is not where Julian expects it to be. The index lists Eva Voss under a different surname, the one her mother used. He finds it because you copied the crossed-out number instead of only the replacement.
In the exchange room, the booth assigned to the original call is full of falling snow.

Not a picture of snow. Flakes drift against the glass and melt on the floor. Behind them is a kitchen with a yellow blind and a clock shaped like a plate. A telephone lies on the counter, its cord twisted around a chair.
Voss sits beside it. He looks younger, not because his face has fewer lines but because he hasn't yet learned how to hold it still. A woman stands by the sink. She is wearing a coat over pyjamas.
“This is the record?” you ask.
Julian nods. “Don't touch either of them. They can't hear us unless we enter the live end.”
You stand just inside the booth. Snow lands on your sleeve and disappears.
The phone rings. Voss reaches for it so quickly he knocks the chair over.
“Eva?”
At first there is only static. The woman at the sink takes one step towards him. He lifts a hand to stop her.
A child's voice says, “Dad?”
You know how this will end. You know he will hear that voice and spend the next year making other people carry what he cannot put down. Knowing doesn't make it easier to watch him close his eyes.
“I'm here,” he says. “I'm here, sweetheart.”
The woman puts a hand over her mouth.
Eva asks about a yellow bowl. You don't understand. Voss does. He says it is still on the shelf. She tells him she put a note underneath it for her mother and forgot to say.
The woman leaves the kitchen. You hear cupboard doors open in another room. When she comes back she is holding a folded piece of paper. She sits down on the floor beside the sink.
Voss keeps asking questions. Where is Eva? Who is with her? Can she see a door? She answers some and ignores others. Once she asks him to stop talking because she is trying to remember something.
He doesn't stop.
“Will you come home?” he asks.
There is a long silence. The snow in the booth falls more slowly.
“Dad. I don't think that's what it's for.”
He looks towards the control box beside the phone. You recognise the diagram on its lid.
“Just stay on the line.”
“I have to go.”
“No. Listen to me. Stay. I'll—”
The call ends.
Voss does not move the receiver from his ear. His wife is still sitting on the floor with the note in her hand. She looks up at him and says his name once.
He presses the callback button.
The booth goes dark.
You find yourself standing in the exchange room with snow melting inside your collar.
Imani says, “That's the real call.”
“Yes,” Julian says.
“The thing in the flat isn't her.”
“Not according to this record.”

You touch the notebook under your arm. The voice said Mum in your kitchen. It knew her cough, her impatient listen, the way she used your name. Voss had one true call. How many false ones would you have answered to hear yours again?

Julian copies the acceptance sequence from the booth's control. It isn't a spell that makes a person obey. It records a permission given for one message, with a clear end. When the caller leaves, the receiving side must let the connection close.
“He kept reopening it,” you say.
Miso sits under the desk, collar almost hidden by his fur.
“You don't get the same person just because you use the same number.”
You save a transcript of the final exchange in the notebook. Imani asks whether you will show Voss.
“I don't know.”
“He might need to hear it.”
“He heard it the first time.”
She considers that without trying to improve it.
On the booth's inside wall, under the fresh layer of snow, a small handprint appears. Then a second. Someone is pressing against the glass from a place you cannot see.
A girl's voice speaks from the disconnected phone.
“Did she like the bowl?”
You turn.
The voice is lighter than Eva's. The question sounds rehearsed.
“I don't know,” you say.
“He wants me to know.”
Imani steps closer to you. Julian reaches for the booth door, then stops with his good hand just above the handle.
You ask, “What's your name?”
The snow stops falling.
After a while, the voice says, “I haven't got that right yet.”

choices.label: Preserve Eva’s original call as evidence

effects.detail: You kept the record of Eva choosing to leave.

choices.label: Clear the playback so it cannot lure anyone again

effects.detail: You cleared Eva’s playback after recording what you learned.

beats.text: Voss's workshop occupies the second floor of a narrow commercial building. The tenant downstairs repairs office printers. Someone has left three machines in the corridor with PLEASE COLLECT written on them in increasingly large letters.
The side entrance is locked. Imani tries the handle once, then steps aside for Julian. He inspects the lock, looks at the screwdriver in her hand and shakes his head.
“It's a proper lock.”
“What did you think it would be?”
“I was hoping for a bad one.”
Miso noses a loose panel beside the stairs. Behind it, a narrow service gap runs up to the next floor. Too small for a person. Large enough for a cat who has several complaints about dust.
“Don't touch anything yellow until I open the door,” he says.
Then he disappears into the gap.

You wait on the stairs. The building hums with ordinary machinery. Below, a printer starts, feeds one sheet of paper and stops. There is an absurd amount of time to think about being arrested. You imagine explaining the bag of chalk and the manual to a police officer. You imagine Leila arriving to collect you and being more disappointed by your poor planning than the offence.
The lock clicks.
Miso sits inside the door with a grey cobweb across his face. Imani lifts it off. He pretends to dislike the help while leaning into her hand.
The workshop is tidy in a way your mother's never was. Drawers are labelled. Cables hang in even loops. On a bench, an open telephone has each removed screw taped beside its original hole.
At the back stands the yellow cupboard.
Julian checks it against the manual. “Main receiver's in the front. We need the independent reader. Behind.”
Imani goes around the side and finds the thin seam in the false back. She works the screwdriver under it, slowly enough that the wood doesn't split.
You watch the door.
On the wall above the bench is a calendar from the year Eva died. The month hasn't been changed. Someone has crossed out the days after her death and stopped halfway through the page.
A telephone rings in a drawer.
Nobody moves.
It rings again.
Imani keeps working. Julian holds the panel steady with his good hand. You press your fingers against the brass feather in your pocket, needing to feel something that doesn't want an answer.
The drawer opens an inch.
“Sam?” Mum's voice says.
You keep your back to it.
“It's okay. He knows you're here.”

The panel comes loose. Behind it is a small brass box with two sockets and a sliding lever. Julian lifts it with both hands, forgets about his injured one, and nearly drops it. Imani catches the lower edge.
The voice in the drawer laughs softly.
“You keep hurting yourselves.”
“Not Mum,” you say, mostly to yourself.
“I know.”
The answer is so unexpected that you turn.

A girl stands beside the open drawer. She has your face, smaller and badly fitted, as if she has remembered the parts without understanding their distances. While you look at her, the features change into Eva's.
“Better?” she asks.
Miso backs against the door. Julian and Imani stand with the reader between them.
“Who are you?” you ask.
She glances at the calendar.
“That's still the difficult one.”
“Where's Voss?”
“He's coming.”
Downstairs, a door closes. You hear shoes on the first flight.
Imani slides the reader into the equipment bag. “Time to go.”
The girl moves between you and the exit.
“You can't take that. He says it makes people leave.”
“It lets them leave,” you say.
“That's what I said.”
The footsteps stop outside the workshop.
Voss tries the handle. It doesn't move. Miso is standing with a paw pressed against a small chalk mark Julian drew beside the hinge.
“Sam,” Voss calls through the door. “I said you could come and speak to me.”
The girl looks towards him. Her face changes again, into a woman you don't recognise, then an old man with a frightened mouth.
“You shouldn't have come in here,” she says, in several voices at once.
The cupboard doors slam open.
Every cable in the room lifts from its hook.
Imani swings the equipment bag over her shoulder and points at the window. You follow her gaze. A flat roof lies three feet below it, across a narrow gap.
You open the catch. Cold air pours in. The girl reaches for you, stops short of touching your wrist, and looks down at her own hand.
“Will he make you stay?” she asks.
You look at the tightening cables. At Miso holding the door. At the spare key hanging beside the light switch where he could never have reached it without climbing into the claim.
“Not if we leave together.”
The girl stares at you. Behind the door, Voss says a name you can't hear clearly.
Miso cries out.
You have to move.

choices.label: Ask the girl what she wants; offer a way out

effects.detail: You asked instead of ordering her to let you pass.

choices.label: Lie that Voss authorised you to take the reader

effects.detail: You used a false instruction from Voss.

choices.label: Strike at her hand with the torch

effects.detail: You tried to strike her in the workshop.

choices.label: Refuse a bargain and demand a path out

effects.detail: You refused to bargain and accepted her displeasure.

beats.text: Imani goes through the window first. She drops onto the roof, turns and holds out both hands for the equipment bag. Julian passes it down, then climbs after it with his injured hand tucked against his chest.
Miso is still at the door.
The cables have reached the floor. One moves over your boot with the deliberate pressure of a finger testing fabric. You lift your foot. It follows.

You take the chalk from your pocket and draw the first release mark on the desk. The line breaks where the surface is covered in varnish. You rub it away and try on the exposed wood beneath a scratch.
The girl's face changes as she watches.
“You know that one.”
“I'm trying to.”
“He doesn't like that one.”
Miso makes another small sound. You don't look at him. If you look at him, you'll hurry the last line and lose it.
“Can you hold this end?” you ask the girl.
She takes a step back.
“Not for him,” you say. “For the cat. Only until he moves. Then you stop.”
She looks at the mark, then at her own hands. The cables around your boots loosen.
“Only until he moves,” she repeats.
“Yes.”
She puts two fingers inside the outer circle. The chalk glows a dull white. You feel a resistance at the edge of the mark, something trying to keep its old shape.
Miso lifts his paw from the door.
The handle turns. You scoop him up, feel his claws close hard around your sleeve, and run for the window.
Voss opens the door behind you.
“Eva.”
The girl pulls her hand out of the chalk circle. You are already on the sill. She looks towards him, then towards the gap.
You don't tell her what to do. You drop.
The roof knocks the air out of your chest. Imani catches your coat, preventing you from sliding into a shallow pool beside the gutter. Miso scrambles out of your arms and crouches against a vent.
Above you, Voss leans out of the window.
“That isn't going to hold the line by itself,” he calls. “You need the calibration I gave Nadia.”
Julian is checking the brass reader. “We have it.”
“No,” Voss says, and for the first time he sounds genuinely alarmed. “You have the original. The load changed.”
The girl steps onto the sill beside him.
“Come inside,” he says.
She looks at the snow collecting on the roof.
“Is that cold?”
“Come inside.”
She lowers herself over the edge. For a moment her shape stretches too far, hand still on the sill while her feet touch the roof. Then she lets go and stands beside you, small and barefoot.
Voss says her borrowed name again. She covers her ears.

The roof door is locked from the other side. Imani goes at it with the screwdriver. Julian holds the bag. You keep your body between the girl and the window, although you're not sure either of you would survive Voss deciding to pull a connection instead of calling.
Then Leila opens the roof door.
All of you stare at her.
“Stairs,” she says. “Building has them. Move.”
She has Dennis behind her. He looks at the workshop window, the girl and the equipment bag, then decides not to ask until everyone is inside.
Downstairs, the printer-repair tenant is standing by his front door with folded arms.
“Do I need to call the police?”
“Yes,” Leila says. “Tell them there's an electrical hazard upstairs. Stay out until someone checks it.”
She doesn't try to give him the rest. You are learning that honesty can be a matter of answering the question someone actually needs answered.
On the street, the girl stops under a lamp. Snow passes through her shoulder, then begins to settle. She holds one flake on the back of her hand and watches it melt.
“It doesn't stay,” she says.
“No.”
“Good.”
Miso approaches her slowly. His collar is twisted to one side. She crouches and offers him her empty hand. He sniffs it without touching.
“What do I call you?” you ask.
The girl looks across the road. On the pavement near a hedge, a small brown bird hops away from the lights.
“What's that?”
“I don't know. A sparrow?”
Imani squints. “Maybe a wren.”
The girl considers both names with obvious seriousness.
“Wren.”
“You don't have to pick now.”
“I want that one.”
“Okay. Wren.”
Her face changes. Eva's features loosen. For a moment she looks unfinished, a person drawn before the lines have been rubbed clean. Then she settles into a face you have never seen before.
Dennis opens the car door. “Can she wear a seat belt?”
Wren looks at it, then at you.
“We can find out,” you say.
In the back seat, Imani passes her a spare pair of gloves. Wren puts both on the same hand, studies the result and waits for someone to explain.
Nobody laughs. Imani takes one off and shows her how.
Wren spends the drive watching the windscreen wipers. Each time they move she leans forward slightly, as if expecting them to take part of the view away.
Dennis notices in the mirror.
“They just shift the water.”
“I can see that.”
“Right.”
“Where does it go?”
He points to the guttering at the edge of the windscreen. She follows the movement all the way down and nods to herself.
At the annex, Leila clears a space in the storeroom. She does not put Wren inside a chalk circle. She tells everyone this before someone can suggest it.
Wren stands by the doorway, looking at the salt marks around the bell case.
“Those hurt.”
“They're for the connection,” Leila says. “We'll keep them away from you.”
“That's what he said.”
Your aunt stops moving.
“Then I'll be more specific. You can sit by the radiator. Nobody will close a mark around you without asking. If we think there's a danger, we'll tell you before doing anything.”
Wren sits on the floor beside the radiator. Miso stays near the opposite wall. They watch each other with matching suspicion.

Julian puts the second reader on the table. He wants to test it immediately. You want to ask Wren about Mum. Imani goes to the vending machine and comes back with plain crackers because nobody knows whether Wren can eat.
She can hold one. She turns it over several times.
“What happens?”
“You bite it,” Imani says.
“After.”
“I don't usually plan that far with a cracker.”
Wren looks at her. Then she smiles, briefly and uncertainly. It is the first expression you've seen on her face that doesn't seem borrowed.
When she bites the cracker, half of it falls into her lap. She stares at the crumbs, annoyed.
You sit on the floor a little way from her.
“My mother,” you begin.
“I know.”
“Did you hurt her?”
Wren puts the remaining cracker down.
“I made the room move.”
“Why?”
“Because she was leaving.”
You have to breathe before asking the next question.
“Did you know what would happen to Julian?”
She looks at his bandaged hand. “I know now.”
Julian doesn't say it's all right. He sets down the wire he is holding and turns towards her.
“You can't do that again.”
“I don't want him to put me back.”
“That's a different answer.”
“Yes,” she says. “I know.”
The room is quiet enough for you to hear the vending machine compressor start in the corridor.
You ask what happens when the Exchange opens fully. Wren rubs a crumb between her fingers until it disappears.
“All the voices come through. Dad says we can find the right one.”
“Voss,” you say, then regret correcting her so sharply.
She looks down.
“Voss says.”
“What do you hear?”
She presses her hands against the sides of her head. “A lot. Some are small. Some are shouting. Some don't know they're finished.”
“Can you stop them?”
“Sometimes. If I use a face they like. Then they listen.”
You think of your own face outside the flat. The note under the glass.
“Why mine?”
“Your mother said it when she was tired. Your name. I heard it so much I thought it was somewhere.”
“What do you mean?”
“A place she was trying to go.”
You look away. Imani moves the cracker packet a little closer to Wren, although she hasn't asked for another.

Julian asks about the changing load. Wren is better at explaining that than at explaining herself. The messages have been accumulating because Voss keeps the receiving lines open. Every unanswered call borrows capacity from the next. Nadia has been holding the group apart with one manual control. By dawn, there will be too many connections for her to distinguish.
“The second reader can ask each one whether it wants to go,” Julian says.
“It can ask,” Wren says. “It doesn't know who's answering.”
“Can you tell?” you ask.
She watches you for a long time.
“Sometimes.”
“If you help—”
“No.”
You stop.
She picks the cracker up again. “You ask and then you do the other thing. You say if, and then I have to.”
Leila sits down beside the table. She does it slowly, with her hands visible on her knees.
“We need to work out what happens to you if the messages leave,” she says. “We can't pretend we already know.”
Wren looks at her. The radiator clicks behind her shoulder.
“I don't want to disappear.”
You cannot promise she won't. The temptation is so strong it makes your mouth feel full of words you shouldn't use.
Instead you ask, “Can we find out before we decide?”
Wren draws one knee up. The glove on her left hand has begun to slip through her fingers. She pushes it back into place.
“Maybe.”
You sit with her while Julian begins testing the reader. For a while nobody asks Wren to do anything useful.

choices.label: Stay without asking Wren to be useful

effects.detail: You stayed without demanding another answer.

choices.label: Press for answers; the deadline is getting closer

effects.detail: You pressed her for answers after she asked you to stop.

beats.text: “Just keep up,” Imani repeats from the alley. “That was the first thing you asked of me. I noticed.”
The reader works on a piece of string. It works on a paper connection. It works on an empty telephone circuit Julian builds from two handsets and a coil of cable Dennis finds in a cupboard.
It fails when Wren puts one finger against the brass socket.
Every light in the storeroom goes out. Leila holds the bell case shut while Julian pulls the contact free. In the sudden dark, somebody knocks a glass off the table. You hear it break near your feet.
“Don't move,” Imani says.
The emergency lights come on. Wren is standing by the door. The borrowed gloves lie empty on the floor.
Julian looks at the reader's indicator. It has counted three thousand four hundred and eleven responses in less than a second.
“That isn't possible,” he says.
Wren backs out of the room.
You follow her into the corridor before anyone can stop you. She is pressed against the wall beside the vending machine, looking down at her hands.
“I said I didn't know,” she says.
“I know.”
“Then stop looking like that.”
You don't know what your face is doing. You make yourself look at the machine instead. Someone has put a packet of crisps in the wrong spiral, and two flavours are wedged together behind the glass.
“I thought we had it,” you say.
“You thought you had me.”
The sentence stings because you can hear the possible truth in it. You had started thinking of Wren as the missing part of the circuit. Not the person who couldn't work out a pair of gloves.
Imani comes out with a dustpan. She sets it against the wall and stands between you, leaving room for Wren to move away.
“We're going to need a different way to count,” she says.
Julian appears in the doorway. “We don't have time to rebuild a whole—”
“Then don't start by telling her she's impossible.”
He closes his mouth.
Leila joins you a minute later. Her palm is red where the case burned through the cloth. She has wrapped it in a damp towel.
“We need the original receiving record,” she says. “The part that establishes who is answering. There should be one for every person the line can name.”
“Wren doesn't have one,” Julian says.
“Then we ask how to make one.”
“Where?”
He knows the answer before your aunt gives it. His face changes.
“No.”
“The witness office.”
“No. The last time I asked somebody down there to fix a record, they took a year of my life I can describe but can't remember.”
“Then we don't give them an undefined payment,” Leila says.
“You make it sound like I forgot to read a form.”
Your aunt goes quiet. The correction lands hard enough that you see her accept it before she answers.
“I didn't mean that.”
“I know. You still said it.”
For a while nobody has a useful next sentence.
Imani takes you into the empty stairwell. You think she wants help moving something, until she closes the fire door behind you.
“Tell me the whole plan.”
“We don't have one yet.”
“Then the whole problem.”
You lean against the handrail. It is cold through the sleeve of your coat.

You tell her what Julian said about the messages entering one person. You tell her how simple it seemed, for a second, to stand where Mum was standing. She doesn't interrupt. When you've finished, she sits down on a stair.
“You were going to swap yourself.”
“I thought about it.”
“And everyone else carries on deciding how to fix things, except now there's another person stuck.”
“You don't know that.”
“No. Neither do you.”
You sit on the step above her. From the storeroom comes the muffled sound of Leila and Julian moving the table.
Imani looks up at you. “You told me Voss hadn't contacted you. I remember asking. I walked into his workshop thinking you had the same information I did.”
“I didn't want you to leave.”
“That wasn't yours to fix by lying.”

You start to explain about the photograph and stop when you hear yourself arranging the facts into something easier to excuse. She waits. Eventually you say, “I wanted you there. I should have asked.”
Imani rubs a mark on the stair with the edge of her glove. “You told me when Voss contacted you. That's why I'm still here. I can deal with a bad plan if I'm actually allowed to know it's bad.”
“I haven't told you every thought I've had.”
“I don't need every thought. I need the bit that puts me on a roof with someone else's cables chasing my feet.”
She takes a deep breath. “I can be your friend without agreeing to everything.”
You look at her. She seems annoyed at having to say friend out loud. You are grateful enough to keep your own face turned towards the rail.
“Okay,” you say.
“Okay isn't a plan.”
“No. But I heard you.”
She studies you for a moment, then gets up. You pick the dustpan up on the way back. There is still broken glass in the room, and somebody needs to clear it before the next emergency.
Wren moves to Imani’s other side when you reach for the door. The broken torch is still in your bag.
Wren keeps her receiving card turned away from you. “You said he gave you permission. I remember.”
Anubis meets you at the bottom of the concrete staircase. He is carrying the driver's cap under one arm. Without it, he looks taller.
Miso stops two steps above him.
“We need a receiving record,” you say.
“So I was told.”
“By who?”
“Someone who does not enjoy being called from a laundry basement.”
You think of the three pens and decide not to ask whether gods complain about each other in a group chat.

Leila has stayed at the annex with Dennis and the bell. Julian came as far as the staircase and stopped. You found him standing with his good hand on the rail, looking at the place where the concrete becomes stone.
“I'll wait here,” he said.
You told him where you were going and when you would return. He checked the time himself. Neither of you called it cowardice.

Now you follow Anubis down a corridor lined with doors. Behind one, someone is grinding grain. Behind another, a woman and a man argue over the ownership of a boat. Nothing resembles the endless fire you expected from the word underworld when you first heard it in a classroom.
At the far end is an office with two chairs. A scale stands against the wall. It is small and practical, its pans scratched from use.
You stop in the doorway.
Anubis notices.
“This isn't the judgment of the dead. Nobody is weighing your heart. Sit down.”
You do. Imani remains standing. Wren stays beside the door with her hands in the pockets of the coat Leila found for her. The sleeves reach past her fingers.
A woman enters from the other room. She wears a plain white dress with a narrow blue border. There is a feather on the desk beside her, its shaft worn smooth by handling.
“You have brought a person whose record is attached to several thousand senders,” she says.
Wren looks down.
“Do you want that record separated?” the woman asks her.
Wren looks at you. You make yourself remain silent.
“I want to know what happens after.”
“Good. Then that is the first question.”
The woman places three blank cards on the desk. On one she writes sender. On one, message. On the third, receiver. She puts a pebble on each.
“When the circuit operates as intended, these remain distinguishable. The message passes. The sender can leave. The receiver can refuse.”
She places the pebbles together.
“Someone has made refusal count as continued attendance. Over time the messages have begun using one another to remain legible.”
“Wren,” you say.
“Is the person who has grown in those connections. That doesn't mean she owns everyone she can hear.”
Wren's hands come out of the coat pockets.
“I didn't ask for them.”
“No,” the woman says. “You didn't.”
You hear Mum's recording in your head. The room, the second reader, the problem of recognising who is actually answering.
“Can she survive without them?”
The woman turns the third card over. On its back is an empty box.

“A receiving record establishes a person independently of what they carry. But it requires the person to claim it. It cannot be issued to Voss's daughter on behalf of somebody who isn't Voss's daughter.”
Wren looks at the box.
“He says names have to be old.”
“People say many convenient things about names.”
Anubis stands at the wall, giving nobody help they haven't asked for. You want him to tell you what to do. You suspect he knows this.
The woman holds out the blank card to Wren.
“What name do you ask us to record?”
“Wren.”
“And whose permission brought you here?”
She looks at you again. Then at Imani, who has been waiting quietly beside her.
“Mine.”
The woman writes the name. The pebble on the third card separates from the others.
Wren gasps. For one second her face becomes empty, too smooth to read. Imani takes a step towards her and stops before touching.
“Can I?” she asks.
Wren nods. Imani takes her hand.
The features return slowly. You recognise the face she chose under the streetlight. Her mouth trembles with effort.
“There are still too many,” she says.
“The record gives you somewhere to stand,” the woman says. “It doesn't remove the people holding the road closed.”

She hands you a copy of the receiving sequence, but gives Wren the original card. You don't reach for it. Wren presses it against her chest as if she has only just found out where to keep something important.
On the way out, you ask Anubis whether the woman was Ma'at.
He looks at you for a while.
“You met someone doing the work of her office. It may be enough to remember the work.”
At the staircase, Julian is still there. He has brought the trolley up from the landing because he couldn't stand waiting without doing anything.
Wren shows him the card.
He looks at it and then at her. Very carefully, he says, “Hello, Wren.”
She grins. It changes her whole face.

c24a.title: A Field With Work to Do

beats.text: The road back from the witness office passes a doorway which wasn't there when you arrived. Beyond it lie fields under a sky too bright for midnight. Water moves along narrow channels. Someone is repairing a wooden gate, swearing at a peg which refuses to fit.
Wren stops.
“There are voices there.”
Anubis looks through the opening. “People. Different matter.”
A woman carrying a basket comes towards the road. She sets it down beside the gate and helps the man hold the wood level. Neither looks particularly interested in you.
You had expected the dead to be waiting. Here they are busy.
“Field of Reeds?” you ask.
“One way of describing a desired place,” Anubis says. “People make places by living in them too.”
Imani watches the man try the peg again. “Does he want a hammer?”
“He wants the peg he made to fit.”
The answer sounds sufficiently ordinary that she smiles.
Wren takes one step through the doorway. You start to reach for her, then stop. She has a receiving record now. She is not a lost cable that must be kept within reach.
“Can we?” she asks Anubis.

c24a~1.title: A Field With Work to Do

beats.text: “For a little while. Don't mistake being welcomed for being expected to remain.”
The ground under your boots is warm. After two days of snow and radiators which never quite heat the room, the sensation is so unexpected that you almost sit down.
The woman beside the gate glances at you.
“Living?”
“Yes,” you say.
“Mind the irrigation channel. Looks shallower than it is.”
Then she returns to the gate.
Wren kneels beside the water. Her reflection appears slowly, the chosen face settling into the moving surface. She looks over her shoulder at Imani.
“Is it supposed to do that?”
“Yes.”
“Mine didn't.”
Imani crouches beside her. Their reflections meet in the water. For a while they stay like that without turning it into a lesson.

You walk to the edge of the field with Anubis. The plants are tall enough to move against your sleeves. Farther away, a group of people are carrying baskets towards a house. One pauses to adjust a sandal, falls behind, then hurries to catch the others.
“Did Eva come here?” you ask.
Anubis looks out over the field.
“That isn't information I owe every person who asks.”

c24a~2.title: A Field With Work to Do

beats.text: “I'm not asking for Voss.”
“I know.”
You let the question go. It is more difficult because he hasn't made it sound foolish.
Near the gate, the peg finally slides into place. The man steps back and tests the wood with both hands. The woman picks up her basket. A task finishes. Nobody asks what must immediately replace it.
Wren comes to stand beside you.
“If I let the voices leave, do I get a place like this?”
Anubis kneels so he is closer to her height.
“You may need to find out what you want after you can hear yourself think.”
“That sounds slow.”
“Sometimes.”
She considers this with obvious dissatisfaction. It is a relief to see her dislike an answer without changing her face to please the person giving it.
Julian waits at the road. He has stayed on the threshold, not because anyone stopped him but because he has discovered a limit he intends to keep. You go back to him before he has to call your name.
“Anything useful?” he asks.
“People doing things,” Imani says.
He looks at her. “Right.”
“No, really. It was useful.”

c24a~3.title: A Field With Work to Do

beats.text: You understand what she means. The waiting messages have made the dead seem like a single enormous need. Seeing someone argue with a gate puts them back into separate lives. You are not trying to satisfy an ocean of grief. You are trying to stop a machine from making one person's absence into everybody else's obligation.
Wren takes the receiving card out of her pocket. She holds it by the edges, away from the water.
“I want to stay with my own name,” she tells Julian.
He nods. “Then we'll set the reader to recognise the record before it accepts the messages.”
“Can I still say stop?”
“Yes.”
“Even if it makes it harder?”
“Yes.”
She puts the card away. The man at the gate has started walking towards the house, carrying the unused pegs in one hand. He doesn't look back.

At the doorway, you notice a figure sitting in the shade, sewing a tear in a coat. For a second your chest tightens. The angle of the head is familiar. The way the person holds the fabric between two fingers.

c24a~4.title: A Field With Work to Do

beats.text: Then they look up. Not Mum. A stranger, mildly annoyed by being stared at.
You apologise and keep walking.
Outside, the night returns. Your boots are cold again. Imani checks the time and sends her dad a message before putting her phone away.
You ask Anubis whether he will come with you.
“No.”
You nod before he has to explain the passengers, the road, the jobs which do not stop because you found a worse one. He looks almost relieved.
At the top of the stair, Miso waits beside Julian's trolley. He sees Wren holding the new card and sniffs the edge.
“Good name,” he says.
“I picked it.”
“I know.”
She smiles. The reflection in the stairwell window smiles with her.
Voss is waiting outside the annex when you return. He stands under the security light with his hands visible and his phone on the pavement beside him.
Dennis has locked the gate. Leila stands inside it with the metal case at her feet.
“I didn't let him in,” she says.
“I can see.”
Voss looks at Wren. For a moment he seems unable to place her. Then his eyes find the borrowed coat.
“Eva.”
“Wren,” she says.
He looks at you. “What have you done?”
“She picked a name.”
“You don't know what she's carrying.”
“Three thousand four hundred and eleven responses,” Julian says. “At least. Your load count was wrong.”
Voss turns towards him. The courtesy drains away.
“That's an instantaneous count. Not an accumulation. Some will be duplicates.”
“And some won't.”
He looks back at the gate. Leila doesn't move.

For a while the two engineers argue through the bars. Voss is better informed about the current load. Julian has the original calibration. Neither has enough on his own, and both know it. You listen until their sentences become so specific that the fear underneath them almost disappears.
Then Voss says, “You need me.”
Leila picks up his phone with a cloth and passes it through the gate.
“We need information you have. That's different from giving you control.”
He takes the phone. His hand shakes once before he closes it around the case.
You show him the transcript of Eva's first call.
He reads the first line and stops.
“I know what it says.”
“Then you know she said she had to go.”
“Don't.”
“Did you ever find the note under the bowl?”
He looks at you as if you have touched him without permission.
“My wife found it.”
“What did it say?”
“That isn't yours.”
“No,” you say. “It isn't.”
You put the transcript away. You hadn't meant to give him that answer. It leaves you both with the strange discomfort of an argument that doesn't finish in the expected place.
Wren comes to the gate. She stands where Voss can see her face clearly.
“I remember the calls,” she says. “I don't remember the kitchen. I know the words because you kept playing them.”
Voss puts one hand on the bars. “You don't have to remember everything at once.”
“I don't want her things.”
“You liked the snow globe.”
“I liked the water moving.”
He looks away.
Behind him, a bus goes past with most of its seats empty. The driver waits at the red light even though there is no traffic. You find yourself staring at the patient, ordinary obedience of it.
Leila opens the gate only far enough to put a chair outside.
“If you give us the revised load sequence, we'll record your contribution. Nobody will pretend you didn't help. You won't operate the reader.”
“And Nadia?”
“We bring her out.”
“The thing inside won't let you close the line.”
Wren steps back from the gate.
You see her face begin to change, and realise she is trying to find one he will listen to. You put your notebook down before your hands can become part of another instruction.
“Wren,” you say, quietly. “You don't have to.”
She looks at you. The face settles.

Voss sits in the chair. For the next twenty minutes he dictates numbers to Julian. He stops twice to correct a figure and once to insist that a particular connection must remain open. Julian writes the correction down and refuses the open connection.
When the sequence is finished, Leila checks it against the original.
“You left out the limit.”
Voss says nothing.
“The return window,” she says. “How long?”
“Seven minutes.”
“Under current load.”
He looks towards Wren, who is sitting on the inside step with Miso beside her.
“Four,” he says.
Julian crosses out seven.

You read the new figure. Four minutes to hold the broken connections, ask the questions the bypass removed, release your mother and bring everybody through. After two days of searching, the answer fits inside a number you can count on one hand.
Voss gets up.
“I can hold the master line. From inside.”
Leila looks at you. This time she doesn't decide in advance which answer you are allowed to hear.
You look at Voss's hands. No cable burns. No grey skin. He has found ways to stay outside the machinery he built.
“If you come,” you say, “you don't get a private channel.”
He nods, reluctantly.
“And if Wren says no, she means no.”
He looks as if he might argue about the name again. Then he picks his phone up from the chair and puts it in his pocket.
“All right.”
You do not mistake the words for a guarantee. Julian writes them down anyway.
Julian looks at the spare connector, then at his bandaged hand. “Tell me before you choose a piece of equipment over the person holding it.”
Julian checks the reader, then meets your eyes. “You pulled me out. I can hold this end.”
Nobody likes rehearsing an emergency. Leila says this while making everyone do it a third time.

Julian has arranged the equipment on two tables. The bell case is at one end, the second reader at the other. Between them lie paper cards representing Nadia, the waiting messages, Wren, the witness, and the operator. He has drawn a little cat on the card for Miso. Miso has been trying to sit on it ever since.
“You're not a load-bearing component,” Julian tells him.
“Good. Finally.”

Voss stands near the door. Dennis watches him from a chair, holding a mug with both hands. There is no realistic reason a retired security officer with a mug should intimidate Voss. It appears to be working anyway.

The first rehearsal fails because you close the holding mark before Imani positions the reader. The second fails because Julian changes a setting with the wrong hand and knocks the lever out of alignment. The third fails because Wren says she isn't ready and everyone else takes too long to stop.
“We stop when she says it,” you say.
Voss turns towards you.
“If we stop at the wrong time—”
“Then we need to know what stopping means before we're in there.”
You hear Leila's teaching voice in your own. It is irritating and useful.

Julian marks three stages on the table with tape. Before the first, you can withdraw. Between the first and second, the system holds temporarily. After the second, the messages have begun to separate; stopping then means choosing another way to contain them.
“What other way?” Imani asks.
“Break the bell,” Leila says. “Sever the crossing. It will get us out, but unfinished messages will lose the only route we know how to reach.”
Wren looks at her card. Her name is written in Julian's cramped hand beside the words independent receiving record.
“And me?”
“The record should keep you separate,” Julian says. “I can't promise what the shock will do.”
You appreciate the honest sentence and hate the uncertainty inside it.

Voss takes a pen and points to the operator's card. “There is one further option. A live receiver could hold the load while the rest of you disconnect. With the bypass removed, it would no longer be forced.”
Everyone looks at him.
“Yes,” he says. “I am aware.”
Mum held it for eleven months. You think about how Voss has arranged the possibility so it sounds newly reasonable now that he has said willing.
Julian puts a second card underneath the operator.
“One person. No ordinary way out. We'd have to build a new receiving point from outside.”
“We don't choose that by accident,” Imani says.
“No,” Leila agrees.

You rehearse again. This time Wren says stop halfway through, and all of you stop. Miso takes his paw off the cat card. Julian lowers the lever. Imani sets the reader down. You open the outer line of the mark without breaking the inner one.
Nothing falls. Nothing is trapped. Wren breathes out and looks almost embarrassed by her relief.
You go again. At the end, Julian checks the timer.
“Three minutes and twenty-eight seconds.”
Imani looks at the table. “Thirty-two spare.”
“Only if nobody argues,” Dennis says.
Voss does not look at him.

Leila packs the equipment. She labels everything in large letters, including the bag containing chalk, which nobody was likely to confuse with anything else. You do not tease her. You have started to understand how much fear can fit inside being organised.

Miso noses the edge of your notebook. A page you haven't read falls open. On it, Mum has sketched several jackal figures in different poses. Beneath one she has written Wepwawet, Opener of the Ways. Beside the name is a note: Ask for a road, not ownership of the road. Courtesy isn't payment. Precision matters.
You read the name aloud carefully. Miso looks towards the door.
“He may be there,” he says. “When the lower route narrows.”
“Does knowing the name help?”
