“Knowing which name to use helps. Don't assume any name gives you command.”
You mark the page with a strip of blue tape. Imani does the same to the release diagram, then hands the roll back without saying anything about whether she trusts you to remember it.

Near midnight, Dennis brings the car around. Leila checks every latch on the bell case. Voss carries the equipment bag under Imani's supervision. Julian signs the archive's paper register before leaving, including an estimated return time.
You look at the blank line after his signature.
“You think they'll care?”
“I will,” he says.
You write your name under his. Your ordinary name, in your ordinary handwriting, with a pen that is running out of ink. Then you close the register and follow the others out.

effects.detail: You learned which divine name and office to invoke.

choices.label: Practise the release sequence once more

effects.detail: You used the remaining time to rehearse the release.

beats.text: The guardian’s gaze stops on the marks of your earlier forced crossing. Knowing a name will not make him overlook how you treated the last road. You will need another way to ask.

The lower entrance is inside a disused service building near the waterfront. The building is Voss's invention before it is a place: temporary walls, false measurements, a real electricity supply someone has continued paying for. From the pavement it looks like something waiting to be demolished.
Leila has brought Dennis to hold the outer line. He checks the chair she sets beside the bell case, tests its legs and sits down.
“Four minutes,” he says.
“Only after we connect the reader.”
“Then tell me when you connect the reader.”
She promises. He takes a small battery timer from his pocket. You are glad someone in the room still believes a timer can do its job without developing a second meaning.
Voss opens the inner door with a key. It leads to a staircase which should come out below ground. Instead it descends beside a wall of dark water. A fish passes on the other side, turns, and is gone.
Imani puts her hand on the rail.
“Does that stay there?”
“Usually,” Voss says.
“Try again.”
“It will hold while the outer line remains stable.”
“Better.”

You go down in single file. Miso moves ahead, stopping at every landing to sniff the corner. Wren stays near the back with Julian. She keeps looking at the water and then touching the card in her pocket.
Halfway down, the lights go out behind you.

Nobody speaks. You take out the torch and point it at the steps. The beam catches water running upward along a crack in the concrete. Something knocks against the wall on the other side, three slow impacts.
Your body knows the rhythm before you do.
Imani looks back. “Not the flat.”
“I know.”
“Just making sure you know.”

The corridor at the bottom ends in a pair of stone doors. A narrow opening lies between them. Through it, you can see the lights of the lower station and, far above those lights, the upside-down shape of Toronto.
Between you and the opening stands a figure carrying a standard topped by a jackal.

He doesn't look like Anubis. Even before you can decide why, the distinction feels important. His posture is forward, alert, the way a person stands before a race begins. When he turns towards you, the end of the standard scrapes a line through the dust.
“No compelled passage,” he says.
Voss steps forward. “The operator is expecting us.”
The standard comes down between him and the doors.
“I heard the words you chose.”
Voss stops.
You find the page in Mum's notebook. The sketch is rough, but the shape of the standard is unmistakable.
Wepwawet looks at the open book.
“The conservator,” he says. “She asked better questions after the first one.”
“What was the first one?” you ask.
“How to get in without being stopped.”
“What should she have asked?”
“How to bring everyone back.”
You hear Julian draw a breath behind you. Wren moves closer to the wall. The pressure of the waiting voices has changed her shape at the edges; her sleeves look too long even for the borrowed coat.
Wepwawet examines each of you. When he reaches Miso, his eyes stop at the collar.
“That one is under claim.”
“Not by choice,” you say.
“A useful distinction. Not yet a release.”
You think of the circle on the kitchen table. You loosened the collar but didn't remove it. Voss has been quiet for too long.
“Let him go,” you tell him.
“He knows the route. If he runs—”
“Let him go.”
The stone doors shift. The gap narrows by an inch.
Voss looks at the standard, then at the cat. He says a word you don't recognise. Miso folds to the floor as the collar loosens completely.
You kneel beside him. He is breathing. His eyes stay open, fixed on Voss.
“You don't have to come farther,” you say.
He gets up slowly. Walks to the edge of the dust line. Looks through the doors.
“I know.”
He crosses back and stands beside your boot.
The opening stops narrowing.
Wepwawet looks at you. “Now ask.”

You could offer the witness receipt and negotiate passage for every person who wants it. You could invoke the office-name you learned, asking him to open a road without claiming it as yours. You could try to force the doors while they are still apart, though the standard hasn't moved an inch and the water beside you is rising.
Or you could turn back. The upper route remains open. There would still be time to cut the outer bell, but not to reach Nadia first.
You put the torch down so both hands are visible.

beats.text: Your knee will not take your full weight. Imani carries the reader while you use the wall. Forcing the earlier crossing has not stayed behind at the doors.

Beyond the doors, the lower station opens around you. It is larger than it was during the first rescue, or you are arriving from a side you didn't see. Rows of switchboards rise towards an arch of dark water. Telephone cables hang between stone columns. Every cable carries a brass label.
The labels are names.
Some are written in letters you recognise. Some use scripts you cannot read. A few are only marks, as if the person writing them had almost forgotten the shape before reaching the end.
Julian stops beside one, not touching it.
“Those aren't all dead callers,” he says.
Leila looks at the label. She recognises the name.
“It's a patient. From the first tests. She declined.”
Voss says nothing.
You turn towards him. “You kept them.”
“I kept the routing information. I didn't send—”
“The line can't tell the difference,” Julian says.

You look down the long rows of names. People waiting for a call. People who refused one. People who once loved someone who used a system that couldn't bear an empty space. The bypass has turned a record into a place to hold them.
Wren presses her hands over her ears.
“They're louder here.”
Imani takes her to the edge of a table, away from the nearest cables. Julian sets up the reader. Leila checks the receiving sequence against the original card. You follow Miso towards the inner room.
Mum is standing this time. She has wrapped a strip of cloth around her hand, but it has burned through in several places.
When she sees you, her face closes with fear before relief can reach it.
“No. Sam, I told you—”
“I listened. Then we found the other reader.”
“Who came with you?”
You tell her. Her eyes reach Voss before you finish.
He stops in the doorway.
“I have the revised sequence,” he says.
Mum looks at the bag, the brass box, Julian's grey hand. She understands more from those objects than you could have explained.
Then she looks back at you.
“You've been learning.”
“You left notes.”
“Not enough.”
“No.”
She accepts the answer. It costs her something; you can see it. You don't soften it before she has time to hear it.
You take her free hand again. This time you don't need to check whether the familiar rough patch is there. Her thumb closes over yours.
“I wanted to call,” she says.
“I know.”

“No. I need to tell you this part properly. I tried. Then I stopped. Every time I thought I could make the next attempt safer, I found another reason to wait. At first it was the right decision. After a while I couldn't tell how much was right and how much was being afraid to hear you ask me to come home.”
“You could have let me ask.”
“Yes.”
Her voice breaks on the word. You look at the burned cloth around her other hand. You are angry with her and afraid for her at the same time, and neither feeling makes room for the other.
Imani comes to the doorway. “We need to put the reader close enough to connect without pulling the hand control.”
Mum wipes her face with her sleeve. “Under the table. There's a shelf. Don't touch the left bracket.”
The instructions give her a way to stand upright again.

For ten minutes you work around her. Julian positions the reader. Imani passes the connectors in the order you rehearsed. Leila renews the holding marks without closing the release side. Miso moves along the floor, checking where the cables pass into the stone.
Voss stands by the master switch. He has the task he asked for and no private line to operate. You watch him whenever his hands move.
Wren comes in last. Mum looks at her face, then at the card she is holding.
“Hello,” she says.
Wren doesn't answer at once.
“You called me the Unnamed.”
“I didn't know what else to call what I was hearing.”
“Wren.”
Mum nods. “Hello, Wren.”
Wren moves closer. “You kept saying Sam.”
“I know.”
“I thought I could bring you there.”
Mum looks at you, then down at the cable in her hand. “That was kind. It was also dangerous.”
Wren's mouth twists. “People can do both?”
“Yes,” Mum says. “I'm finding that very inconvenient.”
It is not a grand explanation. Wren seems to prefer it.
Julian checks the reader. The first indicator glows. The second remains dark.
“We need the actual receiving mark,” he says. “Nadia's. The one Adrian copied.”
Mum nods towards the back of the panel. “His version's there. Mine is underneath.”
You kneel and find the two layers. The false signature is visible on top. Beneath it, scratched into the brass, is the mark your mother drew before the bypass existed.
You copy it exactly. The final stroke curves left instead of right. A small error to build eleven months around.
The second indicator comes on.
Leila calls Dennis through the outer line.
“Connected,” she says.
The timer starts.
At first the reader makes no sound. You can hear the click of the outer timer through Leila's phone, the shallow breathing of the people nearest you, and a relay moving under Nadia's table.
Then every label in the room turns towards the brass box.
You are not sure labels can turn. You watch the movement happen anyway, name after name lifting its lower edge as if caught by a wind you cannot feel.
Julian puts his good hand on the lever.
“First stage.”
You close the holding mark.

The resistance is immediate. Not pain, exactly. The sense that a weight has been placed on the far end of a long tool you are trying to keep level. Your fingers tighten around the chalk. You remember the torn papers on Julian's desk. The forty-one seconds. The way breathing stopped the pieces shaking.
You breathe.
Wren lays her receiving card beside the reader. Her name appears on the blank indicator strip.
Mum starts to open her burned hand.
A cable jerks through the brass loop around her wrist. She cries out and closes her fingers again.
Julian lowers the lever. “Not yet. Something's still returning the refusal as a yes.”
Voss turns towards the master panel.
You see his hand stop over a switch he hasn't mentioned.
“What does that do?”
“Return cache.”
“Turn it off.”
“If we clear it, we lose the stored calls.”
“Turn it off.”
He looks at Wren. The reader is pulling separate voices out of her shape; faces flicker across her skin, too fast to distinguish. At the centre, the face she chose is trying to hold still.
“Eva's in there somewhere,” he says.
You want to shout. You need the breath to hold the mark.
Imani steps between him and the switch. “You heard her leave.”
Voss takes out the photograph. You hadn't realised he still had it with him. He studies Eva's face as if the answer might be written somewhere the camera failed to focus.
Leila's phone says, “Two minutes.”
Mum loosens one finger. Another cable slams against the table. The receiver count doubles.
Wren looks at you. “Too fast.”

Julian has one hand on the lever and the other held uselessly against his chest. He could slow the release, but not while he holds the reader aligned. Imani could reach him, but that would leave Voss alone at the master panel.
Your mark begins to tremble.
Miso puts one paw beside the outer circle. Not inside it. He waits until you nod, then adds his weight to the connection. The trembling eases.
You have seconds in which you can think.

The first option is to finish the separation. It needs a receiver who can remain distinct while the messages move, a route that recognises Wren, and another person to hold the reader steady. You have either earned those things or you haven't. Wanting them now won't put them in the room.

The second is to break the bell. Leila can sever the crossing from outside while Nadia still has enough strength to leave. Wren's new record may hold her shape, but the unfinished voices will be cut away. Some will never reach the people waiting for them.

The third is to take the whole receiving load yourself. Not replace Nadia under Voss's old instruction; choose a new, limited service and give the others time to disconnect. You would stay inside. They could build a way to reach you, but nobody here knows how to bring you home.
Mum sees where you are looking.
“You do not owe me that,” she says.
“I know.”
“You need to know before you choose.”

You look at her burned hand, at Julian's bandage, at the card Wren wrote her own name on. You look at Imani, who has been waiting for you to make a decision she can disagree with and still help you carry out.
Leila's phone says, “Ninety seconds.”
You put the chalk against the last open line.

beats.text: You look past him. Three passengers sit under advertisements for things you have never heard of. A woman with a cardboard suitcase is picking loose threads from her gloves. A boy in a school uniform holds a loaf of bread wrapped in a tea towel. Neither looks at you.
“My mother's missing,” you say.
“That is something that happened. What did you leave?”
The doors wait. The woman stops picking her glove.
You could say the flat. The answer is technically true. You could make a joke and see whether the driver has a sense of humour, though he hasn't offered much evidence.
You look down at the chemistry worksheet still stuck to your boot by a strip of wet tape from the alley.
“I stopped putting her things back,” you say. “When my aunt tidied them away. I used to get them out again. Then it was easier not to.”
Your voice has gone quieter than you want. You hope Imani won't turn towards you.
The driver reaches for a pad of transfers. “Easier to sleep?”
“Sometimes.”
He stamps the paper and gives it to you.
“Rest isn't charged against you here.”
Miso puts his head out of your coat. “Anubis.”
The driver tips his cap. In the window beside him, his reflection has a long black muzzle and upright ears. You look at the real man, then back at the glass.
“Yes,” he says. “Please keep clear of the doors.”
You sit down with the transfer going damp in your hand. Imani sits beside you. For a whole block she says nothing.
Then she points at your boot.
“Question four's wrong.”
“I know.”
“Just checking.”
You peel the worksheet off. Outside, the streetlights stop at the edge of a wide black river.
Mum pushes you towards the door.
“Go.”
“I'm not leaving you.”
“Then you won't be able to come back.”
Imani drags Julian over the threshold. Miso lands beside them. Your mother's hand is still on your coat.
You turn and put your hand over hers. One quick pressure. Then she lets go.
The door shuts against your shoulder.
On the blank wall of the exchange room, you leave a streak of blood from your elbow and a white chalk mark that won't close.

c15_tail.title: The Wrong End of the Rink

beats.text: Afterwards, she takes off her helmet and runs a hand through flattened hair. There is a red mark across her forehead where the padding sat.
“You came.”
“You sent an address.”
“People ignore addresses all the time.”
You think of the notebook and decide not to turn that into an observation.
Her dad goes to fetch the car. She sits beside you and starts undoing the fastening on a shin pad.
“How'd it go?” you ask.
“I don't know. They don't tell you there.”
“You saved that one.”
“I saved several.”
“The one near the end.”
She looks at you. Then she laughs, a quick tired sound.
“Thanks for the detailed analysis.”
You show her Julian's messages. The smile leaves her face, but she doesn't stop undoing the fastening.
“You waited?”
“For once.”
“You can stop making everything a confession. I just asked.”

She pulls the pad free. Under it, her leg is bruised along the shin. You had been thinking of her as the person who arrived carrying a weapon. Looking at the marks, you begin to understand how much work came before she picked it up.

beats.text: Her dad brings the car around. Imani makes you sit in front because her bag occupies most of the back seat. As you drive towards the annex, the heater blows too hot on your wet boots.
“What's wrong with the cat?” her dad asks suddenly.
You look at him.
“The black one. I saw it at the window yesterday. Didn't move for half an hour.”
You consider possible answers. “He's waiting for somebody.”
Her dad nods as if that makes sense.
Outside the annex, he waits until you and Imani reach the door. She turns back and waves. He gives the short two-finger gesture you saw at the rink, then drives away.
Inside, Julian has covered an entire sheet with the same connector drawing. This time he has labelled the missing part.
SECOND READER. INDEPENDENT ACKNOWLEDGEMENT.
You put your notebook beside it.
“Let's go home,” you say. “Properly. All of us.”
You answer before the second ring.

For a moment all you hear is someone breathing too close to a microphone. You are about to ask who it is when the person outside knocks. The breath on the line catches at exactly the same time as yours.
You don't say your name. You learned that much from a school assembly about scams, though the person giving the assembly did not discuss visitors wearing your face.
The voice says, ‘Sam?’
You put the phone on the counter. You want both hands free. You don't know what you expect to do with them.
You hold the power button until the screen goes black. For two seconds the flat is quiet.
Then the phone rings again. The screen stays dark.
You put it on the counter and step away. This feels like the sort of thing that should solve a problem if you do it decisively enough. It doesn't.
The third knock comes from the door.
A voice from the black phone says, ‘Sam? Please. I know you can hear it.’
You recognise the voice, and that is worse than not recognising it.
Eventually you touch the screen. It lights up with the same call still waiting, as though the phone has simply refused to take part in your decision. You answer without putting it to your ear.
‘I'm going to need help,’ you tell Imani. ‘I don't know what kind yet.’
She looks towards the road. ‘Then don't tell me I have to. Ask.’
You try again. ‘Will you come?’
‘Yes.’ She checks the map on her phone. ‘And I'm telling my dad where we are.’
Miso steps around a puddle. ‘Sensible.’
‘You can carry your own phone when you grow thumbs,’ she tells him.
He looks offended. You leave them to establish their own relationship.
‘Just keep up,’ you say. ‘I'll explain when I can.’
Imani stops.
You get three steps farther before noticing. When you turn, she is still standing by the bins.
‘I'm not your employee,’ she says.
‘I didn't mean—’
‘Then use different words.’
You look at the map on your phone. You don't know whether the next street is the safe one. She doesn't either. That is not a reason to pretend she agreed to be instructed.
‘Will you come to the annex?’ you ask.
She considers it. ‘Your aunt asked me to check on you. I'm doing that. We'll see after.’
She walks beside you, leaving more space than before.
‘Tell me what the transfer gives you before I pay,’ you say.
The driver's hand remains open. ‘A record that you entered this road willingly. No claim on your return. No permission to speak for you.’
‘And you keep what I say?’
‘Only the account needed for the crossing.’
You think about it, then tell him you left a kitchen where your mother's things have begun to look like somebody else's clutter. You don't give him every memory attached to that sentence.
He stamps the transfer and gives it to you. ‘Defined terms,’ he says. ‘A useful habit.’
Imani puts her fare away. ‘We're keeping that habit.’
You sit down together. Miso climbs out of your collar, dislodging a considerable amount of fur onto your coat.
‘Nothing,’ you say. ‘I haven't left anything.’
In the window, your reflection smiles. You haven't moved your mouth.
The driver closes his hand. ‘Then I cannot issue the transfer.’
The doors remain open. Beyond them, the staircase is visible. You can get there, but it will not count as a witnessed crossing.
You feel a moment of triumph, followed by the uncomfortable recognition that you have won nothing except permission to leave without the thing you need.
Imani steps down first. She does not look at you until both feet are on the concrete.
‘Was that worth it?’
‘I don't know yet.’
‘Next time, work that out before.’
Miso follows, saying nothing at all.
You try to push past the driver's arm.
You do not get far. The space beyond the fare reader lengthens while your feet stay where they are. Your elbow strikes the rail hard enough to make your fingers numb.
The driver has not moved.
‘You may refuse passage,’ he says. ‘You may not turn everyone else's road into your entrance.’
Imani takes your good arm and pulls you back. You let her. The shame comes before the pain, which is an unpleasant order for either feeling.
At the next ordinary landing, the doors open. No transfer. No blessing. A way out which remains a way out because he said it would.
On the concrete, you unwrap the dressing at your elbow and see fresh blood. Imani has stopped asking whether it hurts.
‘I don't want to give you that,’ you say.
The driver inclines his head. ‘Then use the exit.’
You expected an argument. Getting none makes you hesitate.
Imani steps down beside you. Miso follows. The streetcar remains until you are clear of the doors, then moves away across the river.
‘We still reach the exchange room?’ you ask.
‘We walk farther,’ Miso says. ‘Not every refusal ends the road.’

The steps are steep and your boots are wet. You spend the climb thinking about the question you chose not to answer. You don't decide whether you should have answered it. You are glad the decision was allowed to remain yours.
You show Imani the back of the photograph before putting the notebook away.
‘Those were under Eva's name,’ you say. ‘I copied the crossed-out one too.’
She takes a picture of your page, discovers the photograph comes out blank, and writes the numbers into her own notebook instead.
‘Two copies,’ she says. ‘If one of us drops something off another roof.’
‘We haven't been on a roof.’
‘Give it time.’
You laugh. When the fear returns, you don't have to carry the information alone with it.
You close the notebook before Imani can see the back of the photograph.
‘Anything else he gave you?’ she asks.
‘No.’
The word comes easily. You tell yourself you are checking the numbers before worrying anyone. You tell yourself you will share them when they make sense.
Imani watches you put the notebook away.
‘Okay,’ she says.
You had wanted the lie to end the question. It does. That is not as reassuring as you expected.
You slide the evidence across the desk.
Thoth gives you a receipt with a clear list of what he is retaining. You check the recorder's serial number, though you have never cared about a serial number in your life. Julian checks it too.
‘Copies remain yours,’ Thoth says. ‘The correction will show both the false entry and the evidence against it.’
You nod. You are not buying the disappearance of a bad fact. You are making it possible for someone else to see what happened.
You grab the open book.
It shuts before you can lift it. Your sleeve is caught between the covers. The third pen stops above the page, perfectly still.
Thoth looks at your hand.
‘You came to challenge a stolen authority.’
You let go. The sleeve comes free with a neat tear along the seam.
Julian has gone pale. Imani steps back from the desk. You cannot think of an answer that makes the last five seconds look better.
Thoth copies the public route reference onto a card and puts it beyond your reach. ‘You may take the address. You may not use my witness seal.’
You take the card only after he nods. The walk to the stairs feels very long.
‘I'm keeping the recorder,’ you say.
Thoth withdraws the evidence form. ‘Then I cannot certify the correction.’
‘Can you give us the address?’
He considers the reference number, then writes a public routing entry on a card. ‘A destination. Not proof of your authority to change what happens there.’
You take it. Your mother's voice remains in your pocket. The witness receipt stays on his desk.
Julian does not tell you that you chose badly. He asks you to put the difference in the notebook so nobody later assumes you have something you don't.
You grab Julian's sleeve and pull.
He comes away from the panel with a sharp cry. His hand has gone grey to the wrist. You get his good arm over your shoulder and take his weight before your injured elbow can object.
Behind him, the spare connector remains in the socket. You see it. You know it might have helped. You keep moving.
Julian tries to say your name. You tell him to save the breath until he is through the door.
Imani takes his other side. Together you get him over the threshold.
You reach for the spare connector.
The metal is hot enough to burn through your glove. You pull it free and fall against the panel. Behind you, Imani swears and hauls Julian away from the closing contact.
‘Sam!’
You turn. His injured hand hangs at a wrong, stiff angle. She has his good arm over her shoulder, carrying a weight you chose not to reach first.
You help them through the door with the connector burning in your pocket. It may be useful. It doesn't make Imani meet your eyes.
Julian says, ‘You got it, then,’ in a voice you cannot read.
You put the phone away.
For the rest of the session you watch the puck closely enough to lose it twice. You don't understand every decision Imani makes, but you begin to recognise when she's pleased with one.
When she looks towards the benches again, you are still there.
The archive message can wait until the whistle. You don't pretend waiting was easy. It matters that you chose it anyway.
You show Imani's dad the message and say you need to go. He nods, distracted by a shot at the far end of the rink.

Outside, you call Leila before going to the flat. She meets you there. Together you find the manual before Imani's session finishes. It is a useful hour. You keep telling yourself that while looking at your phone.
Imani's message arrives at eleven thirty: Went looking for you. Dad said you had another thing.
You start an explanation, delete half of it and send the plain version: I left to find the manual. Should've told you myself.
Her reply comes several minutes later. Yes.
When she joins you at the flat, she asks to read the diagram before agreeing to the next part of the plan.
‘You don't have to keep us here,’ you tell the girl. ‘What happens if we leave?’
She looks at the door. ‘He asks why I let you.’
‘You can say we asked you.’
‘That won't be enough.’
You don't tell her it will. Instead you ask whether she wants to come as far as the window and see the roof herself.
She moves aside. Only a little. Enough to let Imani reach the catch without pushing past her.
‘Just looking,’ she says.
‘Just looking,’ you agree.
‘Voss said to let us take the reader,’ you say. ‘It's part of the test.’
The girl's face brightens with relief. Then it tightens.
‘He would have told me.’
You point towards the door. ‘Ask him.’
She turns for long enough that Imani can reach the window. You have bought a few seconds by making another person doubt what she was told.
When the girl turns back, she knows. You can see it before she speaks.
‘You do that too,’ she says.
The cable nearest your boot coils tightly enough to crack the floor tile.
You swing the torch towards her hand, trying to knock the cable away.
It goes through her wrist. The force of your own movement pulls you off balance. You hit the cupboard hard with your injured elbow.
The girl looks down at the place you tried to strike. Her face becomes your mother's for one terrible second.
‘Don't,’ Imani says. You aren't sure which of you she means.
You get up. The torch has broken against the wood. The girl steps back from you, opening a path without offering trust.
Outside the door, Voss begins turning the handle.
‘We're taking the reader,’ you say. ‘I'm not making a deal about my mother.’
The girl watches you. ‘I wasn't asking for her.’
You look at the cable in her hand and realise you heard a threat before she made one.
‘Then let us leave.’
She steps away from the window. ‘You can. I don't have to like it.’
Imani opens the catch. Cold air moves through the room. You keep watching the girl's face, expecting another borrowed one. It stays her own unfinished shape.
For once, nobody makes the refusal mean more than it does.
You offer the witness papers with your hands open.
‘Passage for those who choose it. Return for the same people, if they choose to leave. No replacement required.’
Wepwawet examines the receiving record. He looks at Wren, not at you.
‘Your choice?’
‘Mine,’ she says.
The standard lifts. The stone doors part far enough for the equipment bag.
‘The road is open,’ he says. ‘Keep the terms you named.’
You step through without trying to take a piece of the opening with you.
‘Wepwawet,’ you say, carefully. ‘Opener of the Ways. I ask for a road, not control of it.’
His shadow moves before he does. For a moment the jackal on the standard seems larger than the room.
‘You know which work you are asking for.’
You show him the page in Nadia's notebook. He reads the little correction beside the sketch.
‘She learned.’
‘So are we.’
He turns the standard aside. The gap widens. Knowledge has not made him yours to command; it has let you make a request he can recognise.
Wren goes through beside you, holding her card in one hand.
You push towards the opening.
The standard strikes the floor. The sound knocks the breath from your lungs. You land on your knees, skin burning where the stone scrapes through your jeans.
Wepwawet has not struck you. He has stopped the road moving with you on it. The distinction does not improve the pain.
Imani puts the equipment bag down before helping you stand.
‘You have a route back,’ the god says. ‘Take it if you will not ask for passage.’
You look at the blood on your knee, then at the person holding the door.
‘Passage,’ you say. The word is difficult to get out. ‘For everyone who chooses it.’
He waits until you have named the return terms too. Only then does the opening widen.
You refuse the terms and take the upper stair with the others. Wepwawet does not stop you.

Miso finds an old maintenance return halfway up, a route Adrian once used before the stone doors were installed. It is narrow, flooded and no longer held level. You can reach the lower station, but you won't arrive on a recognised road.

The first section is almost ordinary. Then the water rises to your knees. Imani carries the reader above her head while Julian keeps the receiving card dry inside his coat. You use two holding marks to cross a place where the floor has gone. One collapses before you finish. You strike your knee against a submerged step and keep moving because stopping would leave the person behind you without a place to put their foot.

At the lower end, Miso opens a service panel. You climb into the station soaked, late and unwitnessed. You did not have to accept the god's terms. You have paid for the other road with time and a knee that will not take your full weight.
Imani puts the reader down carefully. “We do not pretend that was free,” she says. You nod before trying to stand.

You ask another question. Wren looks at the empty glove on the floor. “I heard you,” she says. “I said not yet.” You begin to explain the deadline. Imani sets the cracker packet down hard enough that you stop. Nobody has to shout for the room to become uncomfortable. You back away from the question, but Wren keeps watching your hands for the rest of the test.
You put the tested clay figures along the reader’s supports. Each carries one defined segment, then stops. The rehearsal gives you a way to share a load nobody could safely hold alone.
You fit the spare connector into the reader’s empty brace. The component you took gives the load another point of support. Julian checks it carefully before trusting his injured hand near it.
“Clear it,” you tell Voss. “Then leave the switch.”
He doesn't move.
Wren turns towards him. For a moment she is Eva, exactly as she stood in the photograph. You see Voss's whole body lean forward.
Then Wren returns to her own face.
“I could keep doing that,” she says. “Would you ever stop asking?”
He looks at the photograph. At the master panel. At Nadia, trying not to cry out while another cable pulls against her hand.
At last he opens the cache switch.
The photograph tears across its folded crease. He catches both halves and holds them together, although the picture no longer lines up.
The count on the reader drops.
“Imani,” you say.

She moves towards the reader, then stops where you need her. The support comes from the work you prepared and the person still willing to hold the other end. Voss stays where Dennis's voice through the phone tells him to stay. It is an arrangement nobody would have believed possible two days ago.
You open the release side of the mark.

The first voice is a man's. He asks whether his brother collected the tools from the shed. It is so ordinary you almost laugh. Wren looks at the label turning towards her, then at the receiving indicator. A light flashes. The man says thank you, impatiently, as if everyone has taken too long about a simple errand.
His label falls flat.

A second voice follows. Then four. Then enough that you can't separate the words. Wren can. You can see the work in the way she holds her shoulders, the careful pauses between one acknowledgement and the next.
Mum's hand begins to open.
Leila reaches her first. She doesn't pull. She slides a clean piece of cloth under the burned palm and supports the wrist while the cable loosens.
Nadia looks at her sister.
“I'm sorry.”
“Later,” Leila says. Her voice is shaking. “Do that later.”
Mum laughs once and starts crying. The brass loop opens. Her hand comes free.
For a second you nearly let go of the chalk.
Imani says your name sharply. You breathe and hold the mark.
Wren is fading at the edges. Her card remains solid on the table, a small plain rectangle amid the moving light.
“Where do you want to stand?” you ask her.
She looks at the doorway. At the strip of lake visible beyond it. At Miso's paw beside your chalk circle.
“Here. For now.”
“Then keep that.”
She presses one hand to the card. Her face steadies.
A woman speaks through the reader. You recognise Mrs. Bell's voice before the name turns towards you. She does not ask about a pharmacy this time.
“Martin,” she says.
The letter in your notebook grows warm. Somewhere far above you, a receiving line opens for one message. You don't hear the rest. It isn't addressed to you.
Miso lifts his paw. You hold the connection alone for the last few seconds.
The final voice is very quiet. A girl says, “You can put it down now.”
Voss closes his eyes. He doesn't answer. He doesn't reach for a switch. He folds the two halves of the photograph together and lowers his hands.
Julian releases the lever.
Nothing rings.
The labels settle. The cables hang loose. The weight at the far end of your mark lifts so suddenly that you fall onto one knee.
Imani catches the chalk before it rolls under the table.
“Done?” she asks Julian.
He checks the indicator, then checks it again because he doesn't trust a first answer anymore.
“Done.”
Wren stands beside the reader with her hands on the table. She is still there. Her coat is too big. One glove is missing. Her face is hers.
Mum takes a step towards you and almost falls. Leila catches her under one arm. You take the other side, feeling the weight of her ordinary body for the first time since she disappeared.

Miso heads for the stairs without waiting to be told. Wren picks her card up carefully and follows him. Julian carries the reader with both hands; his grey fingers have begun to take colour around the knuckles.
Voss remains beside the master panel.
“Adrian,” Leila says.
He looks up.
“You're coming out too.”
He nods. Picks up the empty equipment bag. Follows.
At the staircase, Mum stops to look back once. You let her. Then you put your hand over hers and help her towards the light.

At the top of the stairs, Dennis gives Mum a blanket before he asks her name. She holds it around her shoulders with the good hand and looks at the ordinary wall behind her as if she can't believe it has stopped being a doorway.
Leila phones for an ambulance. This part she knows how to do. She gives the location, the injuries, the number of people who need assessment. She does not start with the impossible explanation.

Voss sits on a low concrete step. When the police arrive, he gets up without being asked. Leila tells them he has information about Nadia's disappearance and unsafe equipment in two buildings. There will be time later to work out which words can fit in a statement. For now, she gives names and addresses and makes sure they are written down.
Imani phones her dad.

You hear her say, “I'm safe,” then, “I know,” then, “I can't explain all of it over the phone.” She keeps the call going until he reaches her. When he arrives, he hugs her so tightly her feet move off the ground.
Mum watches them. You stand beside her, close enough that your sleeve touches the blanket.
“You can do that,” you say.
She looks at you, uncertain for the first time in a way that has nothing to do with the machinery.
You move first. She wraps the blanket around both of you. Her shoulder is thinner than you remember. You press your face into it and finally stop keeping track of who is watching.
At the hospital, the receptionist asks whether Nadia has identification. Leila produces a folder. Of course she brought a folder. You begin laughing and can't stop until it turns into something else.
Wren waits with Imani in a row of plastic chairs. A nurse asks whether she is family. Wren looks at the card in her hand, then at you.
“Yes,” you say, and then stop before deciding for her. “If she wants.”
Wren thinks about it. “I can wait.”
The nurse gives her a visitor sticker. Wren spends the next hour peeling one corner up and pressing it down again, fascinated by how it stays when she chooses not to hold it.

Julian's hand has regained most of its colour. He still can't bend two fingers properly. Leila makes sure somebody examines them rather than accepting that magical damage must require magical neglect.
Miso stays outside the hospital doors. You find him under a bench when you come out for air. His bare neck looks strangely small without the collar.
“Where will you go?” you ask.
He looks at you. Then at the hospital entrance.
“Where's the clean shirt?”
You sit on the bench. The sun has risen. You missed the moment it happened.

Your phone is full of ordinary notifications: school messages, a discount code, somebody replying to a group chat that has carried on without knowing anything about your weekend. You read each one because you can.
Under them is a new draft call. No number. No caller ID.
The destination is Friday, 02:13.
You don't press it yet. You take the phone inside, where Mum can see it too.
When Imani talks about selection, she reminds you she looked for you after the first session. You listen before offering to come to the next one.
Mum borrows a pen from the nurse and draws the return circuit on the back of a hospital menu. The soup choices get in the way. She works around them.
“The first connection kept a route back to where the claim began. It couldn't close while the receiving instruction was still active.”
“You're saying I called myself.”
“I'm saying you can. I don't know whether you have to.”
The distinction feels like something you learned on the stairs: an open road doesn't decide whether you use it.
You look at the draft call. Friday, 02:13. Your kitchen. The chair at the table. The version of you who hasn't yet learned which details will become important.

You could tell yourself everything. The bell, the notebook, the false signature. You try to imagine receiving that list from an unknown caller and remember how close you came to turning the phone off. Maybe a message can only carry what the person on the other end can hold.
Mum hands back the phone. She doesn't tell you what to choose.
You call.
For one ring you hear nothing. Then the line opens to the sound of your own frightened breathing.
You press your free hand against the hospital chair.
“Whatever happens,” you say, “do not open the door.”
At the other end, a chair scrapes across laminate.
“How do I stop it?”
Your own voice, younger by two days and a great deal else.
“Blue notebook. Kitchen drawer.”
“What?”
“Mum's notebook. Get it. And Sam—”
The connection closes.
You sit with the phone still against your ear. Mum's good hand rests on your sleeve.
“What were you going to say?” she asks.
You look at the hospital menu with its impossible diagram. The floor outside the curtain. Your aunt returning with tea she will insist somebody drinks before it gets cold.
“I don't know. Something useful.”
Mum rubs her thumb across the worn bird patch on your coat.
“You got the notebook,” she says.

Three weeks later, the flat contains more people than it has chairs. Julian brings a folding one from the archive, which he says should not leave the building and has therefore labelled with the building's name in case that helps.

Leila makes dinner. Mum tries to help and is told to sit down. They argue for four minutes about whether chopping one onion counts as rest. You let them. You hadn't realised you missed being annoyed by both of them at once.

Voss is under investigation. There are statements about Nadia's disappearance, equipment records, unsafe access and financial arrangements nobody in your kitchen is qualified to explain. His wife has asked for the original recording of Eva's call. Julian sends a copy through a solicitor. You don't hear what she says when she receives it. You don't need to.

Mum goes to appointments. Some days her hand hurts too much to hold a pen. Some nights she knocks on your bedroom door to make sure you're there, then pretends she needed to borrow a charger. You stop pretending to believe her and let her sit for a while.

You and Leila do not repair everything in one conversation. She starts telling you when she doesn't know something. You start telling her before leaving the building. It is inconvenient for both of you. You keep doing it.

Wren has been living in the annex's spare room while people work out what papers the ordinary world will accept. She comes over wearing a coat that fits. She has learned to dislike olives and asks whether this is a personality or just a food opinion.
“Both, if you mention it often enough,” Imani tells her.

Julian has called his sister. He didn't get the wedding back. He told her why the photographs had become homework. You don't know how much she believed. You know he is going to her house on Sunday and bringing a cake he has been instructed not to choose himself.
Miso sleeps on your chemistry textbook. You move him only when absolutely necessary, which he defines differently from you.
After dinner, Imani stays to help clear the table. Her phone lights up with a message from the selection coach. She reads it twice, then hands you the screen without speaking.
You read the message. Look at her. She is trying very hard not to smile before you do.
“You got it.”
“Conditional. Still training.”
“You got it.”
She grins properly then. You shout for Leila, who comes in carrying a wet plate and complains that you frightened her before joining the celebration.

Later, when everyone has gone, you find a small paper bird on the fire escape. Wren made it from the blank end of an old archive form. Its wings are uneven. You bring it inside and put it beside Mum's blue notebook.
Your phone rings.
Imani. She left her gloves under the chair, and she would like you to stop telling people she cried at the message, because she didn't.
You look towards the kitchen, where Mum is trying to make toast without setting off the alarm.
You answer.
THE END
“Leila. Tell Dennis.”
She looks at the reader, then at Nadia's hand. You see her understand the whole choice before she speaks into the phone.
“Sever the outer circuit. On my count.”
Wren takes one step away from the table.
“Will it hurt?”
“I don't know,” you say.
It is the hardest answer you have given her.
Imani goes to her side. “You can hold my hand if you want.”
Wren nods. The borrowed faces move more slowly across her skin, as if the voices are listening too.
Julian makes sure the second reader is detached from the main line. His good hand is precise. His injured one shakes.
Mum opens two fingers. The cable jerks. You add the last of the chalk to the holding mark and press the point down hard enough to hurt.
“Now,” you say.
Through Leila's phone comes a sharp metal crack.
Nothing happens for half a second. Then every label in the room lifts at once.

The sound is not a scream. It is thousands of unfinished syllables cut short, words losing their ends. A request, an apology, somebody asking where a book has been put. You hear fragments and understand none of them well enough to keep.
Mum's cable goes slack.
Leila pulls the brass loop open with both hands. Nadia cries out. You turn towards her and miss the moment Wren falls.
Imani catches her before she reaches the floor. Wren's face has gone pale and difficult to see. Her receiving card lies on the table. You pick it up and put it in her hand.
“Wren.”
She doesn't answer.
You say it again, not as an order, just as the name you know belongs to the person in front of you.
Her fingers close over the card.
For several seconds, all of you wait. You can hear Mum breathing behind you, uneven and too fast. Julian has put the reader down to kneel beside Imani. Miso stands at Wren's feet, his back arched.
Then Wren opens her eyes.
“Quiet,” she says.
Nobody tries to tell her that's good.

The station begins to change. Without the connections holding its different parts together, the rooms no longer fit. The doorway to Nadia's table becomes a narrow arch. The far switchboard slides towards a wall which wasn't there before.
“We leave,” Julian says.

He doesn't wait for agreement. He lifts the reader, checks that Imani has Wren, and moves towards the stairs. You help Leila support Nadia. Miso leads, stopping whenever the floor changes under his paws.
Voss stands alone beside the master panel. The switches have gone dark. He is pressing one with the end of his thumb, over and over, without enough force to move it.
“Come on,” you tell him.
He doesn't hear you. Or he does and doesn't know what to do with the words.
You go back far enough to take his sleeve.
“We're leaving.”
He looks down at your hand. Then at the empty panel. He comes without resisting.

On the first landing, the wall of water moves inward. You feel cold drops on your face. Imani shifts Wren's arm higher across her shoulders and keeps climbing. Julian goes backwards up two steps so he can guide her feet.
The lower station folds away beneath you.
You don't watch it go. Your mother is heavy against your side, and every time she breathes you can feel her ribs move through the coat.
At the top, Dennis stands beside a bell broken into two uneven pieces. The button has rolled under his chair.
He looks at the people coming through the door and counts silently. You see his lips move.
“All out?” he asks.
Leila looks back at the narrowing stair.
“All of us,” she says.
It is accurate. You hear the part it leaves out.
For the first hour, Wren cannot bear to have anyone speak behind her. She turns at every sound, checking that it comes from a single mouth.
Imani sits where she can be seen. Julian brings water. Leila checks Nadia's burns, then Wren's hands, though there are no marks she knows how to treat.
Voss asks whether he can speak to Wren. She says no. He sits on the far side of the service room until the police come.

You tell them which buildings to check. Leila gives the statements she can make without guessing. Dennis shows them the broken bell. You keep thinking of the names in the lower station, trying to remember more than fragments.

At the hospital, Mum falls asleep halfway through asking a question. You sit beside the bed with her good hand between both of yours. When a nurse needs to check her blood pressure, you stand up too quickly and nearly fall.
“Eat something,” the nurse says.
You want to tell her that food isn't going to address the situation. Then you remember Leila has been saying similar things for eleven months, and you go to find a sandwich.
Wren is sitting by the window. She has removed the visitor sticker because the name field was blank. Julian gives her a pen. She writes WREN in large careful letters and puts the sticker back.
“Are they gone?” she asks.
“The messages?”
She nods.
“I don't know where they went.”
“You can say you don't know without looking like you're asking me to fix it.”
You sit down at the other end of the row. Outside, a hospital shuttle waits with its engine running.
“I keep trying to remember the names.”
Wren looks out of the window. “I remember some.”
“Can we write them down?”
“Later.”
“Okay.”
You sit without asking again.

When Imani's dad arrives, she goes to him at once. You watch them through the glass panel in the corridor door. She is speaking quickly, trying to explain enough. He listens with one hand on the back of her head.
Mum wakes in the afternoon. She asks for you, then for Leila, then whether everyone got out. You give her the answer Dennis got.
“All of us.”
She closes her eyes. “That's not a small thing.”
“I know.”
You do know. You also know why it doesn't feel like enough.
On your phone, the last unknown call has vanished from the log. In its place is an unsent return connection. The destination is Friday, 02:13.
You show it to Mum. She studies the screen for a long time.
“The bell's gone,” you say.
“The route was made before it broke,” she says. “One message. If you want.”
You look at her, lying in a hospital bed in Toronto. Alive. You look at the numberless call and think about what you could have said to the person you were two days ago.

You take the unsent call into an empty part of the corridor. The hospital is beginning its evening routine. Visitors put on coats. Staff change shifts. Somebody wheels a cart past you and says excuse me twice before you notice you're in the way.
You sit down where you can see Mum's curtain.

The destination waits on the screen. Friday, 02:13. You remember what the voice said. You remember the terror of hearing yourself from a day that hadn't arrived. The reserved date on the line was never the date of the speaker. It was the next place the old receiving instruction could put a message.
Now you can give it the voice it was waiting for.
“Whatever happens,” you say when the call connects, “do not open the door.”
You hear yourself move in the kitchen. You give the instruction about the notebook. You start to say one more thing, and the line ends.
For a long time you look at the dark screen.

You want to believe the warning could make the ending different. That another version of you could find one more piece, persuade one more person, hold the chalk a little steadier. You cannot send a second call. The socket is closed.
You go back to Mum.

Three weeks later, you and Wren sit in the annex with a stack of blank cards. She names the voices she remembers. You write them down. Sometimes she knows a whole name and a sentence. Sometimes only a sound. You leave spaces instead of filling them with guesses.

The letter from Mrs. Bell lies beside the cards. Its address has faded but remains legible where Imani copied it. Whether you deliver it or keep it waiting is a decision the broken bell can no longer make for you.
Mum comes to help when her hand allows it. She is home now. The phrase still catches you by surprise. You hear her drop a spoon in the kitchen and feel relief before irritation can reach the sound.

Her return does not arrive as one clean happy thing. There are appointments, police interviews, questions from school and neighbours. She tires quickly. You get angry over small things because the large ones are hard to begin. Once you snap at her for moving your notebook, and she puts it back without telling you how lucky you are to have her there. Later, you apologise for the way you said it. You don't apologise for needing your things left alone.

Leila has started using a shared calendar. She calls it practical. You suspect it is also her way of letting you see the plans before they become instructions. You put your own appointments in, reluctantly. Neither of you celebrates this development out loud.

Wren is quieter than she was before the bell broke. She no longer changes faces when she is frightened. Instead she goes very still and asks people to stop talking for a minute. Usually they do. She is learning which people need reminding.

Julian's hand is recovering. He has told his sister about the wedding memory. She sent him a voice message three minutes long, mostly calling him an idiot and asking when he was coming round. He keeps it backed up in three places.

Imani has a decision from the selection coach. She tells you in person. You go to her next session and sit at the right end of the rink this time, where she can see you without turning her head too far.

Voss does not come to the annex. His part in Nadia's disappearance and the dangerous equipment is being investigated. You don't know whether any ordinary court can account for the rest. You know Leila gave them every record she could explain, including her own signature on the early tests.
One evening, Wren stops halfway through a name.
“What if I forget?” she asks.
You look at the cards. At the spaces you left.
“We'll keep what we've got.”
She nods, but she isn't entirely reassured. You don't add a prettier sentence to make yourself feel more helpful.
At home, Mum has burned the toast. The alarm is going off. Miso is shouting from the windowsill as if he has personally discovered a fire nobody else has noticed.
You open the kitchen window. Cold air enters. The alarm stops.
Mum stands in the middle of the room holding a plate with two black rectangles on it.
“I'm out of practice.”
“You were never good at toast.”
She looks offended for a second, then laughs. You put the plate in the sink and get out the cereal.
Your phone rings. A schoolfriend, asking whether you want the notes from chemistry. You look at Mum. She nods towards it and goes to fill the kettle.
You answer.
THE END
You ask Julian to describe the choice one more time.
He looks at Mum. At Leila. At Imani, who has gone very still.
“One receiver,” he says. “No forced continuation. We disconnect every other claim. The station becomes a place you operate, not a place that owns everyone attached to it.”
“Can you reach it from outside?”
“Yes. With the second reader.”
“Can you get me out?”
He doesn't look away.
“I don't know.”
Mum says your name. You turn towards her. She is trying to let go of the cable, trying to make the other choice possible before you finish considering this one.
“Don't do it because you're my child,” she says.
You kneel beside the panel. You could still break the bell. That choice remains. The thought helps you keep the next words steady.
“I'm not taking the old instruction.”
Julian lowers the lever enough to open a blank receiving line.
You take the brass feather from the box. Mum's fingers close around your wrist.
For a moment you stay like that, neither pulling away nor giving in. Her hand is warm above the burned cloth. You want another hour in the kitchen. You want her to complain about your hair again.
“I need you to keep looking,” you tell her.
She closes her eyes. When she opens them, there is no agreement in her face. There is understanding, which is different and harder to accept.
“I will.”

You write your name beside the new receiving slot. Then you say what you accept, as carefully as Leila taught you to define a connection. Only the waiting messages. No authority over their senders. No new compulsory calls. A line that can be reached from outside without placing the caller under claim.
The feather warms in your hand.
Julian records each condition. Wren repeats it, listening for a response the rest of you cannot distinguish. Imani checks the page before letting you move to the next line.
The indicator shows your name.
You close the holding mark around yourself.
The load arrives slowly enough for you to know you could still stop before the second stage. You say that aloud. Julian confirms it. You take one more breath.
“Continue.”
Mum's hand comes free.

She folds to the floor. Leila catches her. You want to go to them, but the room has changed its sense of distance. The table is near and also impossibly far away. You can hear a woman asking for her son. A boy wants to know whether his bread is still warm. An old man is angry about a set of tools.
You say wait, and the voices wait. Not forever. Long enough for you to understand the difference.
Julian disconnects the old receiving loop. Wren takes her card from the table. Her face steadies as the borrowed voices move towards you instead.
Imani comes close enough that you can see the worn tape on the spare stick she brought from home.
“You don't get to turn into a job,” she says.
“I'll try not to.”
“No. Pick something ordinary. Something we can ask you about.”
You look around the room. There is a chair near the switchboard, its seat split along one seam.
“The chair's terrible.”
She nods, furious and crying now. “We'll start with that.”
Miso stays beside your chalk mark. Leila tells him to come. He looks at her and lies down.
“Miso,” you say.
He puts his head on his paws. “I'm not under claim.”
You cannot make him leave without contradicting the whole connection you just made.
Mum reaches you one last time. You are not sure whether she crossed the room or the room allowed her. She puts her uninjured hand against your cheek.
“I am going to be very difficult about this,” she says.
You laugh. It hurts. “I know.”

Then Leila takes her towards the stairs. Julian carries the reader. Wren stops in the doorway and raises her hand. Imani follows last, looking back until the angle of the corridor takes you out of sight.
The station settles. It is smaller now. No borrowed corridors. No locked inner room. Just the table, the switchboard, the chair and a cat who has chosen to remain.
You sit down. The split seam catches your coat.
At the first socket, a light comes on.
You check the receiving conditions before lifting the handset.
“Hello,” you say. “You can leave a message. You don't have to stay.”
You begin by trying to answer every light. Within an hour, you understand why Mum made lists.

Some people want a message carried. Some want to know why they were called. Some have been waiting so long they are angry before you speak. You tell each one what the line can do. You don't promise a receiver will answer.
Miso finds a cupboard with a dry blanket inside and carries it to the foot of your chair. He spends a long time arranging it, then lies down on the bare floor beside it.
“You could use that,” you tell him.
“So could you.”
You pull it over your knees. The station is cold when nobody is moving through it.
At noon, the second reader opens a controlled line from the annex. Julian is on the other end. You can hear him testing the connection by reading out the time, then a list of objects on his desk.
“Can you hear all that?”
“Yes.”
“Good. Don't answer when it's just the test tone.”
“I have learned one or two things.”
“I'm writing them down anyway.”
Mum comes on after him. She is in hospital. You can hear the soft bleep of a monitor and Leila talking to someone farther away.
“Have you eaten?” she asks.
You look around the station. You aren't hungry. You don't know whether that is reassuring.
“I need to find out how that works here.”
“I've got the manuals.”
“Of course you have.”

For a while neither of you says anything else. You listen to the room around her. A trolley passes. Someone laughs. A plastic curtain slides along a rail. You would never have chosen a hospital as a place to miss so badly.
“Sam,” she says at last. “I shouldn't have needed you to do this.”
“I know.”
“You can be angry about it.”
“I am.”
She breathes out. You are glad you said it before it became one more thing neither of you could ask.

Wren comes on briefly. She tells you that snow melts at different speeds depending on what you put it on. She has been conducting tests on a windowsill, a glove and the sleeve of Julian's cardigan. He has objected to the cardigan.
Imani is last.
“The chair,” she says.
“Still terrible.”
“Good. Means we're talking to the right person.”
You laugh for the first time since the stairs closed. Miso raises his head to check the sound, then puts it down again.
After the call ends, you find a new line waiting on the board. It is not connected to a person. It has your number written beside it, in handwriting you recognise as your own.
The destination is Friday, 02:13.
You examine the routing stamp. One day after arrival, not the day of departure. The date your phone showed. Nadia's manual calls it a reserved receiving slot.
You've spent two days wondering who was on the other end. Now the empty socket waits for a voice.

You check the return line against Mum's manual before using it. One message, back to the point where the first claim began. The date is a reserved receiving slot, a place in the route rather than a promise about which day the speaker belongs to.
It explains the wrong date on your phone. It does not make hearing your own breathing less strange.
“Whatever happens,” you say, “do not open the door.”
You give yourself the notebook. The kitchen drawer. You start one last sentence and the line closes before you know how to finish it.
Miso lifts his head from the blanket.
“Done?”
“I think so.”
“Then somebody's waiting.”
You turn to the next light.

The first week is hard in ways you didn't rehearse. You miss being able to leave a room because you are tired of it. You miss food you can complain about. You miss the sound the flat's radiator makes before it warms up.
You do not miss school until Julian brings your chemistry work through the controlled line. Then you miss the whole building, including the corridor where the lockers never close properly.

Mum calls every evening. Sometimes she talks about the receiving point she is trying to build. Sometimes she tells you what she bought at the supermarket. When she begins explaining an experiment without asking how you are, you interrupt her. The first time, she is hurt. The second time, she catches herself.

Leila keeps the calls from becoming only research. She asks about sleep, then listens when you say you don't know whether you are sleeping or merely resting between messages. She writes it down without pretending the answer is reassuring.

Imani brings a chair. Getting it through the controlled route takes most of a Saturday and an argument with a door which appears not to recognise furniture as an authorised visitor. She refuses to leave it behind. When it finally arrives, the seat is scratched but intact.
“Sit,” she says.
You sit. It is an excellent chair.
She stands beside you for a while, looking at the board. A light comes on, then another. You let them wait. That is permitted now.
“I got the place,” she says.
“At the selection?”
She nods.
You get up so quickly the chair scrapes backwards. She laughs, then you are hugging her, and for a minute the station contains a celebration which has nothing to do with being brave.

Wren visits with Julian. She is learning to write messages which belong only to her. Most are questions. Some are complaints about how many ordinary words have more than one meaning. She brings Miso a knitted mouse. He ignores it until she leaves, then carries it to the blanket.

Voss has not tried to call. The investigation continues above. Nadia has supplied the original manuals and signed a statement about her own work. Julian tells you the records will be complicated. You believe him. You have developed a strong dislike of stories which end when the person responsible looks sad enough.

You help a few callers each day. You turn down requests that would make somebody else answer by force. You ask the right question before accepting a message. Sometimes a receiver refuses. The refusal is recorded, and the line closes. No one is punished for it.
At the end of the third week, Mum reaches the station through the visitor route. Not a voice. A person. She has a bag of sandwiches and several pages of calculations held together by a bulldog clip.
She puts the calculations down first.
“How are you?” she asks.
You look at her hand. It is healing. You look at the sandwiches, the ordinary grease showing through the paper.
“Angry,” you say. “Sometimes. Homesick.”
She sits in the old chair, which Imani repaired rather than throwing away.
“Tell me.”
So you do. Not everything. Enough to begin.

Later, she shows you the calculations. There may be a way to divide the station's role among several consenting operators, each with a defined shift and a way out. It is not ready. It is not a promise she can safely make. She tells you both facts before asking whether you want to help test it.
You read the first page. Make a correction in the margin. Ask a question.
Mum smiles at the familiar impatience in your voice.
On the switchboard, a light comes on. You check its conditions, then lift the receiver.
“Hello,” you say.
Miso closes his eyes in the warm patch beside your new chair. Mum opens her notebook. Somewhere above you, people are having an ordinary evening, and the controlled line home remains open.
THE END
The hallway is empty.
At least, it was when you locked the door.
Then your phone vibrates.
No caller ID.
The call is dated tomorrow.
